MUQATIL:2:164/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:164/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:164/r1.claim: The Meccan unbelievers demanded a sign, asking Muhammad to turn al-Safa into gold; the verse points instead to God's created signs.

MUQATIL:2:164/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:164/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:164/r2.claim: The ships benefit people in their livelihoods; rain revives the earth after its dryness and spreads creatures across it.

MUQATIL:2:164/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:164/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:164/r3.claim: The winds alternate between punishment and mercy, and the clouds are held between heaven and earth as signs for people to affirm God's oneness.

FARRA:v1p96/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p96/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p96/r1.claim: With تساقط البيوت, رفع on بعضها follows the semantic subject البيوت, while genitive follows its surface form; the implied meaning is that the houses fell onto one another.

FARRA:v1p96/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p96/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p96/r2.claim: Raising بعضها is clearest after a pronoun; genitive after a pronoun sounds poor when a visible noun follows, though genitive remains possible. The same alternation applies to an accusative verbal construction.

FARRA:v1p96/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p96/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p96/r3.claim: The winds change direction: south, north, qabūl, and dabūr; this is their تصريف.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p67#3/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p67#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p67#3/r1.claim: Al-fulk means ships and has the same form in singular and plural.

TAB-FULL:v3p10/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r1.claim: The night and day differ by succeeding one another: when one departs, the other takes its place, as 25:62 also says.

TAB-FULL:v3p10/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r2.claim: Zuhayr's verse uses khalfa for things that alternate or follow one another, illustrating the meaning of “ikhtilaf.”

TAB-FULL:v3p10/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r3.claim: Layl is the plural of layla, and layali adds a yāʾ in the plural as do forms such as rubāʿiyya, thamāniya, and karāhiyya.

TAB-FULL:v3p10/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p10/r4.claim: Arabs rarely pluralize nahār because it is like light, though nahr is attested; a poet uses it, and anhar would be a regular diminutive plural.

TAB-FULL:v3p11/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p11/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p11/r1.claim: Al-fulk means ships; one form serves for singular and plural and may be masculine or feminine. The feminine allati suits ships set in motion and thus running.

TAB-FULL:v3p11/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p11/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p11/r2.claim: The ships benefit people at sea.

TAB-FULL:v3p12#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p12#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p12#2/r1.claim: Batha means to disperse, as when a ruler sends troops out; dabba is an active participle from dabba, “to move,” and names living creatures other than winged birds because they move on the earth.

TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r1.claim: The grammar suppresses the agent and attaches the verbal noun to its object; God directs winds by sending them as pollinators, making them barren, or sending them as destructive punishment.

TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r2.claim: Qatada says God can make winds a sterile, nonpollinating punishment for those against whom they are sent.

TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r3.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
TAB-FULL:v3p12#3/r3.claim: Some grammarians interpret this as winds coming from different directions, but al-Tabari says that describes their variation, not God's directing them; he allows the sense of God's directing their different courses.

TAB-FULL:v3p12/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p12/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p12/r1.claim: The water sent from heaven is rain; reviving the dead earth means restoring it, making it flourish, and bringing forth vegetation. “Death” means ruined, barren ground with its provision-producing growth cut off.

TAB-FULL:v3p13/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r1.claim: Clouds is a collective noun from cloud, whose adjective appears masculine singular as with “date” and “palm”; its name likely describes clouds pulling one another, from the verb for dragging. 13:12 likewise uses the collective.

TAB-FULL:v3p13/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r2.claim: These are signs and proofs that the creator and originator of all things is one God; people of reason understand the evidence for His oneness.

TAB-FULL:v3p13/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r3.claim: God directs proofs to rational, discerning people because they alone are addressed by commands and prohibitions and held accountable for worship, reward, and punishment.

TAB-FULL:v3p13/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r4.claim: The argument addresses polytheists who already acknowledge God as creator but worship idols alongside Him; their denial does not erase the signs of a creator and incomparable governor.

TAB-FULL:v3p13/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p13/r5.claim: The signs enumerate God's exclusive blessings: sun and moon sustain livelihood, rain restores land, livestock provide food and clothing, and winds and clouds support crops, people, and herds; 30:40 challenges whether partners can do this.

TAB-FULL:v3p16/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p16/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p16/r1.claim: The verse addresses people who acknowledge God as creator yet associate partners, rather than atheists and materialists; even the smallest sign could persuade all people, but al-Tabari omits further detail to avoid length.

TAB-FULL:v3p5/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p5/r1.speaker: بعضهم
TAB-FULL:v3p5/r1.claim: One explanation says the verse was revealed to answer idolaters who challenged the claim that their God is one after hearing 2:163.

TAB-FULL:v3p5/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p5/r2.speaker: عطاء
TAB-FULL:v3p5/r2.claim: Ataa reports that Quraysh asked how one God could suffice for everyone after 2:163, so this verse was sent to show He is God and creator of all.

TAB-FULL:v3p5/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p5/r3.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v3p5/r3.claim: Another explanation says polytheists asked Muhammad for a sign, and the created order itself supplies clear evidence of God's oneness to anyone who reasons.

TAB-FULL:v3p7/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r1.speaker: أبو الضحى
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r1.claim: Abu al-Duha reports that after 2:163 the polytheists demanded a sign, prompting revelation of 2:164.

TAB-FULL:v3p7/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r2.speaker: أبو الضحى
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r2.claim: In another report, the polytheists marveled at the declaration of one God and demanded proof if Muhammad was truthful.

TAB-FULL:v3p7/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r3.speaker: عطاء بن أبى رباح
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r3.claim: Ataa ibn Abi Rabah reports that the polytheists asked the Prophet to show them a sign, and this verse was revealed.

TAB-FULL:v3p7/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r4.speaker: سعيد
TAB-FULL:v3p7/r4.claim: Sa'id recounts Quraysh asking Jews and Christians about Moses's and Jesus's miracles, then asking for al-Safa to become gold; the Prophet sought respite, and the verse points to creation as a greater sign.

TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r1.claim: Creation means originating and bringing the heavens and earth into existence after they did not exist; al-Tabari says he has already explained why “earth” is singular.

TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r2.speaker: بعض الناس
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r2.claim: One theological view treats a thing's creation as something other than the thing, reasoning that God's will is a created thing through which other things exist.

TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r3.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r3.claim: A second view says creation is an attribute of a thing, neither identical with it nor separate from it; making it separate would entail an endless regress of created attributes.

TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r4.speaker: آخرون
TAB-FULL:v3p8#2/r4.claim: A third view identifies a thing's creation with the thing itself, so “in the creation of the heavens and earth” means in the heavens and earth.

ZAJJAJ:v1p236/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p236/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p236/r1.claim: Creation’s scale and variety prove God’s oneness: the unsupported sky, varied terrain and minerals, changing winds that pollinate clouds, and all earthly creatures cannot be made by another.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r2.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r2.speaker: ابن كثير
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r2.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads الرياح in the plural at this verse and four other listed places: 15:22, 18:45, 30:46, and 45:5.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r3.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r3.speaker: نافع
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r3.claim: Nāfiʿ reads الرياح in the singular in twelve listed places, including this verse and 7:57, 14:18, 15:22, 18:45, 25:48, 27:63, 30:46 and 30:48, 35:9, 42:33, and 45:5.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r4.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r4.speaker: أبو عمرو
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r4.claim: Abū ʿAmr matches Nāfiʿ's distribution except that he reads singular only at 14:18 and 42:33 among those twelve; the remaining listed places are plural.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r5.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r5.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r5.claim: ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir follow Abū ʿAmr's distribution of singular and plural forms.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r6.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r6.speaker: حمزة
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r6.claim: Ḥamza reads the plural in 25:48 and 30:46 and the singular in the other listed places.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r7.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r7.speaker: الكسائي
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r7.claim: Al-Kisāʾī follows Ḥamza except that he also reads the plural at 15:22.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r8.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r8.speaker: author
IBNMUJAHID:v1p172/r8.claim: The readers agree on singular when the word lacks the definite article.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r1.claim: Quraysh asked the Prophet to turn al-Safa into gold so they could strengthen themselves against their enemy; God offered this with a threat of unmatched punishment if they disbelieved, but the Prophet asked to summon them gradually, and this verse was revealed because they already saw greater signs.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r2.claim: Wahb transmits a prayer attributed to Ezra describing creation and the opening of the treasury of light and wisdom, from which night and day were made to alternate by God's command.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r3.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r3.claim: Al-Suddi glosses al-fulk as a ship; Sa'id ibn Jubayr is reported to give the same meaning.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r4.claim: Abu Hurayra says that every drop of rain descends according to a measure.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v1p273/r5.claim: Ikrima says the water descends from the seventh heaven and each drop lands on a cloud like a camel.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r1.speaker: عبد الله
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r1.claim: Abdullah describes resurrection bodies being formed from water sent from beneath the Throne, compared to men's semen, just as plants grow from soil; he recites the verse about reviving the earth.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r2.speaker: النبي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r2.claim: The Prophet explains resurrection by comparing it to land that is barren, then fertile, then barren, then fertile again.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r3.claim: Qatada says that just as God revives dead earth with water, He will revive people on Resurrection Day.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r4.claim: Al-Suddi explains “spread” as “created”; Muqatil ibn Hayyan is reported to hold the same gloss.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r5.claim: Qatada says God can make winds and clouds a mercy, including winds that pollinate clouds and spread mercy, or send barren winds as punishment.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r6.speaker: أبي بن كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v1p274/r6.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b distinguishes Qur'anic plural “winds,” which denote mercy, from singular “wind,” which denotes punishment.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r1.speaker: كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r1.claim: Ka'b says clouds act as a sieve for rain, preventing falling water from damaging what it lands on; Ibn Abbas confirms he heard Ka'b say this.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r2.speaker: كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r2.claim: Ka'b also says that seed descends from the sky, explaining why different plants grow in different years; Ibn Abbas says he heard him say it.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r3.speaker: أبو الضحى
IBNABIHATIM:v1p275/r3.claim: Abu al-Duha explains that the signs from the creation of the heavens through this verse are signs for people who reason.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r1.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r1.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r1.claim: The singular reading treats the wind as punishment, supported by the Prophet's prayer for winds rather than a wind.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r2.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r2.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r2.claim: The plural reading distinguishes winds of mercy from winds of punishment; the singular is reserved for punishment and the plural for mercy.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r3.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r3.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p91/r3.claim: The winds are named by their relation to the Kaaba: front is ṣabā/qabūl, right south, left north, and rear west; west is a punitive wind, the rest merciful.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r1.speaker: ابن كثير
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir reads الرياح in the plural here and at four other places, using singular الريح elsewhere in the listed set.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r2.speaker: نافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r2.claim: Nafi reads الرياح in the plural in twelve locations, including this verse; Abu Amr, Asim, and Ibn Amir also have the plural here.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r3.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r3.claim: Hamza and al-Kisai read the singular here: Hamza pluralizes only two other locations, while al-Kisai adds al-Hijr 15:22 to those two.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p248#3/r4.claim: The Qays describe four principal winds—north, south, east, and west—and call a wind between two directions a nakba; Abu Zayd illustrates the east wind with poetry.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r1.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r1.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi locates the south, east, north, and west winds by the rising or setting points of Suhayl, the Pleiades, and Banat Na'sh.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r2.speaker: الأصمعي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r2.claim: Al-Asma'i gives a different compass description: south runs from Suhayl to dawn, north faces it, and the winds from behind and opposite the Kaaba are west and east.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r3.speaker: ابن الأعرابي والأصمعي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r3.claim: A wind between two named winds is a nakba; al-Asma'i also applies the term when one of the four veers from its course, with plural nakb.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r4.speaker: الطوسي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r4.claim: Another account places the south from Yemen and north from Syria, calls south al-Azyab or al-Na‘ama, and gives north the names Mahwa and Jarbiya.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r5.speaker: الطوسي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r5.claim: The hot, drying quality called hayf belongs to the south and west winds; north and east do not have it.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r6.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r6.speaker: الطوسي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p250/r6.claim: Mahwa is a name for the north wind because it wipes away and disperses clouds; other names include مسعا and نسعا.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r1.speaker: الطوسي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r1.claim: The sterile wind does not pollinate clouds; pollinating winds stir clouds by God's permission and fertilize trees, while ذاريات winds scatter dust.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r2.speaker: الطرماح
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r2.claim: In al-Tirmah's وصف, a pollinating wind is the south and a barren one is the north; the adjectives mean possessing fertilization or its opposite, not active participles.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r3.claim: In الحجر 15:22 لواقح means ملاقح (fertilizing winds or winds that are fertilized); the form omits an augment, as poetry also omits it in a verbal noun.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r4.speaker: الأصمعي
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r4.claim: People dislike the cold north wind because it removes clouds, but welcome the warm south wind for bringing clouds, rain, fertility, and relief.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r5.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p252/r5.claim: The phrase للقح الجنوب is parsed as لإلقاح الجنوب, with the augment omitted from the verbal noun and the noun annexed to its agent.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r1.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r1.claim: The plural وتصريف الرياح is clearest because each wind equally signifies divine oneness and is directed for people's benefit; a singular may still denote the generic wind.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r2.claim: If all winds were subjected to Solomon, الريح signals their multitude; if one particular wind was subjected, the singular is definite by reference.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p255/r3.claim: The wind sent against ‘Ad and the wind sent against the Confederates was one wind, supported by verses and the report that the east wind aided the Prophet while the west wind destroyed ‘Ad.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r1.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed for a wind to come as plural winds rather than a singular wind; al-Farisi takes this to distinguish mercy from punishment.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r2.claim: Plural winds suit mercy and singular wind punishment: he links the prayer to the merciful herald winds in al-Rum and the singular sterile wind sent to ‘Ad.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r3.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r3.claim: Wind can denote a generic class containing both mercy and punishment; as a generic noun it can refer to all winds or only some members, as in the passage about passing by the people of Lot.

FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v2p257/r4.claim: In Quranic usage, وما يدريك normally leaves the matter unspecified, whereas وما أدراك is followed by an explanation; he cites the Hour and the Resurrection as examples.

THALABI:v2p32/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r1.claim: Al-fulk means ships, and the same form can denote one vessel or many.

THALABI:v2p32/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v2p32/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas associates plural winds with mercy and the singular wind with punishment.

THALABI:v2p32/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r11.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v2p32/r11.claim: The Prophet is reported to pray that a blowing wind be made plural winds of mercy, not a singular wind of punishment.

THALABI:v2p32/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r12.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r12.claim: The word الريح can be grammatically masculine or feminine.

THALABI:v2p32/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r13.claim: Clouds are called sahab because they move as if dragging themselves along.

THALABI:v2p32/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r14.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r14.claim: The signs are indications that let rational people know these things have a creator and maker.

THALABI:v2p32/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r15.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v2p32/r15.claim: The Prophet warns of woe for anyone who recites this verse without reflecting and learning from it.

THALABI:v2p32/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r2.claim: Masculine agreement follows the singular form and feminine agreement the collective sense.

THALABI:v2p32/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r3.claim: Ships benefit people by carrying riders and trade, livelihoods, and other goods sought.

THALABI:v2p32/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r4.claim: The water sent down from heaven is rain.

THALABI:v2p32/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r5.claim: The earth was revived after its dryness and barrenness.

THALABI:v2p32/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r6.claim: Batha means to spread and scatter.

THALABI:v2p32/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r7.claim: The changing of winds means turning them into easterly, westerly, northerly, and southerly winds.

THALABI:v2p32/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p32/r8.claim: Another interpretation is that God turns the winds between mercy and punishment.

THALABI:v2p32/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p32/r9.speaker: حمزة والأعمش والكسائي وخلف
THALABI:v2p32/r9.claim: These readers recite الريح in the singular; the remaining readers use the plural الرياح.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r1.claim: The raised heavens, unsupported, with their moving sun, moon, and stars are signs of divine unity and power.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r10.speaker: شريح
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r10.claim: Shurayh says every wind that rises does so either to make a healthy person ill or a sick person well.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r11.speaker: أبو معاذ
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r11.claim: Abu Muadh reports that Hafsa's codex read al-arwah, spirits or winds, instead of al-riyah, winds.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the name wind as deriving from its bringing relief hour after hour.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r2.claim: The earth's seas, rivers, minerals, trees, plains, and mountains are signs of God's power.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r3.claim: Night and day differ as one arrives and the other departs from places people cannot know.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r4.claim: Al-fulk means ships; singular and plural share one form, and the word may be masculine or feminine.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r5.claim: Ships are signs because they carry their loads independently and reach their destination.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r6.claim: Rain usually comes when needed and stops when no longer needed, which is a sign of God's power.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r7.claim: Rain revives earth through flowing rivers and springs and through growing trees and crops; both sustain living creatures.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r8.claim: Dabba names animals for their movement over the earth; their varied creation, purposes, and instinctive needs show divine power.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p216#2/r9.claim: The winds shift among directions without a known cause or destination, and their changes can bring benefit or harm.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r1.speaker: ذو الرمة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r1.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's verse uses al-arwah as a poetic term for winds.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r2.claim: Al-musakhkhar means subdued or made subject; clouds show divine power through their formation and dissolution, suspension without supports, and direction wherever God wills.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p218/r3.claim: The verse gathers signs that guide rational people to God's unity and power; God calls them to reflection rather than giving bare information.

QUSHAYRI:v1p81/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p81/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p81/r7.claim: God discloses Himself to rational seekers through signs of power, existence, and lordship in His acts; every created thing points to divine unity and offers a path to Him.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p47/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p47/r2.speaker: عطاء
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p47/r2.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports that Quraysh objected to the claim of one God, so God sent the signs in creation as evidence for people who reason.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p47/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p47/r3.speaker: أبو الضحى
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p47/r3.claim: Abū al-Ḍuḥā reports that idolaters challenged the claim of one God and demanded a sign, prompting the verse about signs in creation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r1.claim: After 2:163 declared God one, idolaters were astonished and demanded a sign from Muhammad; this verse was revealed in response.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r2.claim: The listed created signs teach how to reason to the Maker and His oneness, directing people to contemplate signs and created things.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r3.claim: The wondrous, precise, coherent acts of creation prove divine unity: two creators would necessarily interfere, and could not both possess equal perfection.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r4.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p452/r4.claim: The heavens are plural because they comprise different kinds, each heaven unlike another; earth is singular because it is all soil.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r1.claim: Falak derives from turning; it can mean anything round, the seven celestial orbits where stars run, a rounded girl's breast, a spindle whorl, or a ship that turns easily on water.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r2.claim: Falak serves as both singular and plural: it is masculine when singular and feminine when plural, because its form suits either use.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r3.claim: Other broken plurals share their singular's form, including هجان, دلاص, and شمال; speakers distinguish number from context rather than morphology.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r4.speaker: سيبويه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r4.claim: For singular falak the vowel resembles the bāʾ of برد, while plural falak has the plural pattern of حمر; identical sound can represent distinct meanings and origins.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r5.speaker: سيبويه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p455/r5.claim: The identical vocative form يا منص can result from different truncation and vowel processes, illustrating that one pronunciation may carry distinct meanings.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r1.claim: God subjects ships to travel on the water and keeps their heavy, weighty bodies afloat; the same subjection appears in 14:32.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r2.claim: Ships benefit people through riding and carrying commerce; the carrier is relieved and the recipient benefits from delivered goods.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r3.claim: Earth's death means drought and dryness: without rain it does not grow, and rain revives it, as in the quivering, swelling earth of 22:5.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r4.claim: The Arabs call stillness death; the poet's wish that wind die means cease moving, the opposite of the earth's motion when rain makes it quiver.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p456/r5.claim: Calling drought death and rain's removal of it revival makes the paired wording agree with itself.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r1.claim: Bath means spreading and dispersal; related uses include God spreading people in 4:1, scattered moths in 101:4, disclosure of a secret, and grief that cannot remain concealed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r10.speaker: غيرهما
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r10.claim: Others derive لم يرح from رحت أريح.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r11.speaker: أبو عبيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r11.claim: He says the rāʾ should have fatḥa and begins to cite a supporting poem.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r2.claim: Every creature moving on earth is meant, including humans and all other created beings.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r3.claim: The phrase means God's turning the winds; the verbal noun is annexed to its object, a common construction, and الرياح is the plural of الريح.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r4.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r4.claim: The singular الريح has a wāw root changed to yāʾ by the preceding kasra; the small plural أرواح keeps wāw, while the large plural رياح changes it, like ديمة/ديم.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r5.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r5.claim: He derives الريح from روح because winds usually bring spiritual relief, while their absence brings distress; the original wāw is confirmed by أرواح.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r6.speaker: زهير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r6.claim: His verse uses الأرواح alongside rains, illustrating the plural form and supporting the root's wāw.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r7.claim: A prophetic report says a neglectful governor will not smell Paradise's fragrance, found even a hundred years' journey away; the segment then records disagreement over the vocalization of لم يرح.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r8.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r8.claim: He holds the correct vocalization is لم يرح, derived from أراح أريح.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r9.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p458/r9.claim: He reads the rāʾ in لم يرح with fatḥa.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r1.claim: In Qur'anic usage, the question وما يدريك generally leaves the matter unexplained, unlike وما أدراك, which is followed by an explanation, as in 42:17 and 101:3,10.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r2.claim: Taṣrīf means turning or reversal; صريف can be milk after its foam turns away, milk stopped before foaming, or a stallion's tusks as it turns them against each other.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p465/r3.claim: The winds turn through the four directions and alternate between mercy and punishment, heat and cold, gentleness and violent force.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p466/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p466/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p466/r1.claim: Clouds are named for gliding through the air.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p466/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p466/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p466/r2.claim: Subjection means making compliant; the subdued clouds obey God.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:163-164/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:163-164/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:163-164/r2.claim: Creation, alternating night and day, ships serving trade, rain reviving barren land, creatures, changing winds, and subdued clouds are signs of God's oneness.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:163-164/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:163-164/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:163-164/r3.claim: God teaches people to infer the Creator and divine unity by reflection on these signs, yet some still associate partners despite knowing idols cannot do these things.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r1.claim: Fulk means ships in either singular or plural; it is feminine when plural and masculine when singular, as the cited verses illustrate.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r10.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r10.claim: Cloud is named for its rapid movement, as though it were being dragged; the signs teach rational people that these things have a creator.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r11.speaker: وهب بن منبه
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r11.claim: Wahb says the origin of thunder, lightning, and clouds is unknown.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r2.claim: Ships are a sign through God's subjection of them to travel on the water while carrying loads without sinking; people benefit by riding and trading.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r3.claim: The rain's 'heaven' may mean clouds, where God creates water before it falls, or the familiar heaven, from which it descends through clouds to earth.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r4.claim: Water revives the earth after its dryness and barrenness, while God disperses every kind of creature across it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r5.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'wind' in the singular; most readers use the plural, Abu Ja'far uses plural elsewhere, and readings vary except in the agreed cases cited.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r6.claim: Wind shifts among south, north, east, west, and intermediary directions, and can be gentle, violent, hot, or cold.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas calls wind and water the greatest of God's forces.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r8.speaker: شريح القاضي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r8.claim: Shurayh says every wind brings either relief to someone ill or illness to someone well.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r9.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177#2/r9.claim: One account says eight winds divide into four of mercy and four of punishment; another names the merciful winds as the bearers, spreaders, scatterers, and senders.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r1.claim: The heavens are plural because each is a distinct kind, while the earth is singular because all earths share the substance of soil.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r2.claim: The heavens signify their height without pillars and their sun, moon, and stars; the earth signifies its breadth and its trees, rivers, mountains, seas, minerals, and plants.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r3.claim: Night and day differ by succeeding one another; the verse parallels the description of them as alternating turns.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r4.speaker: عطاء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r4.claim: Ataa explains their alternation as differences in light and darkness and in their increasing and decreasing lengths.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p177/r5.claim: Night is mentioned before day because it came first; the author cites the image of day being stripped from night.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r1.claim: Night and day alternate, each following the other, as in the verse about their succession.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r2.claim: The ships benefit people through their cargo, or through other benefits they provide.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r3.claim: One parsing coordinates spreading creatures with what God sent down, within the relative clause describing the water.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r4.claim: Alternatively, spreading creatures coordinates with reviving the earth: rain revives it and fertility sustains its creatures.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r5.claim: The winds vary in direction and in being hot, cold, violent, gentle, barren, or fertilizing.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r6.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#2/r6.claim: Another reported interpretation says the winds alternate between mercy and punishment.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r1.claim: God subjects clouds to winds, turning them through the air by His will and raining wherever He wills.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r2.claim: Rational observers recognize these signs as evidence of God's immense power and striking wisdom.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r3.claim: The Prophet warns readers who recite this verse without reflecting or learning from it; no grading is supplied.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p236#3/r4.claim: Readings include al-fulk with two dammas and the singular الريح.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r10.speaker: عطاء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r10.claim: When the verse was revealed in Medina, Quraysh in Mecca asked for evidence and a sign of the claim.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r11.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r11.claim: Quraysh demanded a sign such as turning al-Ṣafā into gold; after the warning of punishment, the Prophet asked to defer the demand.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r12.claim: Creation of the heavens and earth means bringing them into existence; another interpretation refers to their created form and arrangement.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p231#3/r13.claim: Night and day succeed one another in turn, as in 25:62.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r1.claim: The verse may also mean that night and day differ in their qualities.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r10.claim: Ships serve commerce and other needs such as raids and pilgrimage; benefit is specified because ships can also bring harm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r11.claim: The rain revives the world and brings forth plants and provision; “spread” means distribute and extend, and “creature” encompasses animals generally.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r12.claim: He rejects excluding birds from “creatures,” citing lines by al-Aʿshā and ʿAlqama that describe birds’ movement as dabīb.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r13.claim: “Diversifying the winds” means sending them in varied forms, including barren, fertilizing, cold, victorious, destructive, and from different directions.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r14.claim: The Qur’an usually uses plural winds with mercy and singular with punishment, except the good wind in Jonah; this distribution is common in speech.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r2.claim: The continuation of the poem cited as evidence for the alternation of night and day describes gazelles and young animals taking turns.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r3.claim: A second poet’s lines likewise use “khilfa” for alternating periods, including ants’ foraging and resting.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r4.claim: Night is the plural of layla and may form layālī with an added yāʾ, as in karāhiya and farāhiya.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r5.claim: For legal usages such as oaths, day runs from dawn to sunset, based on the Prophet’s explanation to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r6.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r6.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the day begins with the sun’s first rays; al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl instead starts it at sunrise and excludes the preceding time.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r7.claim: The Prophet’s statement to ʿAdī is decisive for the legal definition of day; the broader lexical sense begins when daylight spreads.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r8.claim: The cited verse and poetic example support the broad daylight sense, in which daylight has spread out.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p232/r9.claim: “Fulk” means ships; singular and plural share the form, while “two ships” shows the dual between them, and singular fulk is masculine.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r1.claim: The Prophet prayed for winds in the plural and against using the singular form.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r10.claim: Al-Kisāʾī follows Ḥamza and additionally reads the plural in al-Ḥijr; all readers use singular where the word lacks the definite article.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r11.claim: Clouds are named for gliding along, and their subjection means God moves them from place to place; Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī gives the derivation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r12.claim: These phenomena show that a Creator exists; reason also establishes that the Creator must be one, since multiple creators could disagree.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r2.claim: Punitive wind is one integrated, forceful body, while merciful wind is gentle and broken into currents.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r3.claim: Riyāḥ is a vowel-conditioned form from rīḥ; the form aryāḥ is not accepted, and ʿUmāra ibn ʿAqīl withdrew his usage after Abu Ḥātim corrected him.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r4.claim: Nāfiʿ reads the plural in twelve locations; Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir use singular at Ibrāhīm and al-Shūrā 42:33; other readers have their own distributions, while all use plural here.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r5.claim: Clouds are named for gliding along; God’s directing them from one place to another is their subjection.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r6.claim: Nāfiʿ reads the plural in twelve locations including this verse, with the cited locations elsewhere in the Qur’an.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r7.claim: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir read the singular at Ibrāhīm and al-Shūrā 42:33, and plural elsewhere.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r8.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads plural at five locations—this verse, al-Ḥijr, al-Kahf, the first al-Rūm occurrence, and al-Jāthiya—and singular elsewhere.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p233/r9.claim: Ḥamza reads plural in al-Furqān and the first occurrence in al-Rūm, singular elsewhere; al-Kisāʾī agrees and adds al-Ḥijr.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r1.speaker: محمد
TABRISI:2:164#2/r1.claim: A prophetic report says the east wind brought victory, while the west wind destroyed Aad, supporting a particular singular wind.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r2.claim: Creation means bringing something into existence according to a measure without copying a model; only God can properly be called creator.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r3.claim: Scholars differ over خلق as a verbal noun: some take it as willing the thing; others as a name for an abstract, determined state such as existence or origination.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r4.claim: The term creation can also denote the created object, just as رضا can denote what is approved, though source and created thing are not identical meanings.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r5.claim: The heavens are plural because revelation identifies them as seven; saying earth in the singular avoids suggesting that one heaven alone is meant.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r6.claim: The heavens are not one uniform class: each has its own appropriate governance, whereas earth resembles one kind whose plural would imply differing kinds.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r7.claim: اختلاف means either the alternation of night and day, each following the other, or differences of kind such as black versus white.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r8.claim: Night is darkness following day; day is expansive brightness. Night has a count noun, while day generally functions like a mass noun, though a rare plural occurs.

TABRISI:2:164#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#2/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#2/r9.claim: The poet's verb أنهرت witnesses the sense of making wide or opening broadly, applied to the widening of a tear in cloth.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r1.claim: الفلك names ships in either singular or plural; it also means the celestial orbit or any circular thing. The lexicographers differ whether it names rotation or the seven celestial layers.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r2.speaker: صاحب العين
TABRISI:2:164#3/r2.claim: One lexical view takes الفلك to be the rotation itself; another takes it as the seven layers containing the stars.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r3.claim: Some say السماء can mean clouds because anything above another is its sky; Ali ibn Isa says clouds may be vapors rising from earth, a possibility neither reason nor revelation rules out.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r4.claim: The known heaven is the roof above earth, and the root of سماء conveys height; layers can be sky relative to what lies below and earth relative to what is above.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r5.claim: A sea is a broad expanse of water wider than a river; benefit is pleasure, joy, or what leads to either, and painful means can benefit when they yield pleasure.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r6.claim: Land lives through plant growth and dies through dryness; broadcasting means dispersing, and dabbah covers every created creeping thing though common usage means riding animals.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r7.claim: تصريف is turning and varying; cloud is named for its dragging motion, while subjugation, taming, and making easy are near synonyms.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r8.claim: The four winds are north, south, east, and west; their names and directions are defined in relation to the qibla, with intermediate winds between them.

TABRISI:2:164#3/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#3/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#3/r9.claim: Broadcasting means dispersing, and grief is called بث because it divides and burdens the heart.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r1.speaker: أبو داود
TABRISI:2:164#4/r1.claim: Abu Dawud's verse describes clouds as impregnated and brought to rain by the south wind; للقح الجنوب means that the south wind impregnates them.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:2:164#4/r10.claim: When people cursed a strong wind, Ibn Abbas told them not to curse it but to ask that it be mercy rather than punishment.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r11.claim: Clouds are controlled by God and moved as he wills from one land and place to another.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r12.claim: The phrase people of understanding can include all rational people, whether or not they infer from the signs; another reading limits it to those who do infer.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r2.speaker: زهير
TABRISI:2:164#4/r2.claim: Zuhayr's verse calls the cold north wind مشمولة, reflecting that people dislike its cold and its dispersal of clouds; the term extends to anything disliked.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r3.claim: The passage answers disbelievers asking what proves that their deity is one: the listed created phenomena are signs of one creator.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r4.claim: The heavens and earth were originated with measured design; night and day succeed one another or differ in kind, color, and length.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r5.claim: Ships carry cargo and benefit people through travel, trade, and earnings; benefit is singled out because the list counts blessings, even though ships can also harm.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r6.claim: All exegetes take water from the sky as coming from the direction of heaven; another view says the intended source is clouds.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r7.claim: Rain makes dead land fertile after drought and failed growth; alternatively, it revives inhabitants by providing food and other necessities of life.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r8.claim: God disperses every kind of animal over the earth by creating animals in scattered places.

TABRISI:2:164#4/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#4/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#4/r9.claim: Qatada explains varying winds as some bringing mercy and others punishment.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r1.claim: Change and susceptibility to increase or decrease show that the heavens and earth are originated; their origin implies a creator unlike them, since created bodies need an unoriginated maker and an infinite regress is impossible.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r2.claim: The heavens' exact order and integration indicate a knowing, wise maker.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r3.claim: The regular cycles and changing lengths of night and day, tied to sun and moon, indicate a managing knower whose precise acts admit no disorder.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r4.claim: Water's delicacy allows ships to move, while winds drive them against the water's course; such provision for human benefit comes from a benefactor unlike humans or bodies.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r5.claim: Rain descends in separate drops, is held in the air despite water's downward nature, and falls in needed measure and season; this proves a powerful, wise administrator.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r6.claim: Fruits, plants, provisions, and animals display diverse tastes, colors, scents, benefits, and harms, demonstrating perfect power and wisdom.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r7.claim: Animals' different forms and anatomies, with intricate tissues and organs, show their maker's power, wisdom, and beneficence.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r8.claim: Winds vary by direction, heat, cold, gentleness, violence, barrenness, and pollination; no creature could change one direction into another.

TABRISI:2:164#5/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#5/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#5/r9.claim: Clouds suspended without a cord or support prove the power of the incomparable God.

TABRISI:2:164#6/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#6/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#6/r1.claim: The phenomena evidence God's pre-eternity and eternity, perfect power, and marvelous creation: he is unmade, powerful, knowing, living, and untouched by change or affliction.

TABRISI:2:164#6/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#6/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#6/r2.claim: God's knowledge reaches even a speck in heaven or earth, and he is hearing and seeing.

TABRISI:2:164#6/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#6/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#6/r3.claim: The signs show God as benefactor, giver of incomparable blessings, and the only deity deserving worship.

TABRISI:2:164#6/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164#6/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164#6/r4.claim: The verse requires rational examination and inference as the path to knowing God, and invalidates reliance on imitation.

TABRISI:2:164/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164/r1.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read الريح singular here; the other readers use the plural, with detailed distributions varying across the Qur'an.

TABRISI:2:164/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164/r2.claim: Abu Ja'far reads الرياح plural throughout except in al-Dhariyat; Abu Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Amir, and Asim have it plural in ten specified locations.

TABRISI:2:164/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164/r3.claim: Nafi has twelve plural readings, Ibn Kathir five, and al-Kisa'i three; Hamza agrees with al-Kisa'i except in al-Hijr.

TABRISI:2:164/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:2:164/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas associates plural winds with mercy and singular wind with punishment.

TABRISI:2:164/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r5.speaker: محمد
TABRISI:2:164/r5.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed that a blowing wind be made merciful winds rather than a destructive wind.

TABRISI:2:164/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164/r6.claim: The prophetic prayer likely alludes to winds sent as good news and to the barren wind sent against Aad; Qur'anic wording can mark a particular sense.

TABRISI:2:164/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r7.speaker: أبو علي
TABRISI:2:164/r7.claim: Abu Ali prefers plural الرياح because each wind is like the others as evidence of divine unity; singular can express a generic class, as in common sayings.

TABRISI:2:164/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164/r8.claim: The singular wind against Aad is one particular wind, supported by the parallel description as a violent, cold wind and by the report about the west wind.

TABRISI:2:164/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:164/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:164/r9.claim: The Qur'anic formula ما يدريك is generally left unexplained, unlike ما أدراك followed by an explanation; wording can signal whether the matter is disclosed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r1.speaker: السدي عن ابن مسعود وابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r1.claim: Polytheists asked the Prophet for the Safa hill to become gold as proof of his truthfulness, and this verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r10.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r10.claim: Rain revives the land, but one water produces plants with differing species, flavors, colors, and forms; this refutes nature as their cause, since one uniform cause should produce uniform results.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r2.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r2.claim: After Quraysh asked God to be described and then requested a sign of the one God, this verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r3.speaker: عطاء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r3.claim: When Quraysh questioned how one God could suffice everyone after 2:163, this verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r4.claim: The unsupported heavens and the earth, with its fruits, level plains, and anchored mountains, display their Creator.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r5.claim: Night and day each comes into being after not existing, then passes away after existing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r6.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r6.claim: Fulk means ships, and its singular and plural have the same form.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r7.speaker: اليزيدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r7.claim: The singular of fulk is fulka; the word may be masculine or feminine.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r8.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r8.claim: Fulk means ships and can be singular or plural; Arabic has several such forms, including words for ships and round things.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p167#3/r9.claim: The sea means abundant water, and ships carry livelihoods that benefit people.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r1.claim: Baththa means dispersed or spread throughout the earth.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r2.claim: The winds' changing directions and qualities include north, south, west, east, punishment, and mercy.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r3.claim: The subdued clouds display four signs: their beginning, disappearance, unsupported suspension, and movement wherever God wills.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r4.speaker: ابن كثير
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r4.claim: Ibn Kathir reads الرياح in the plural at five listed locations, including this verse, and the singular elsewhere.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r5.claim: Abu Ja'far reads الرياح in the plural at fifteen listed locations; Nafi and Abu Amr mostly follow his pattern with stated exceptions.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r6.speaker: حمزة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r6.claim: Hamza reads الرياح as plural only in al-Furqan and the first occurrence in al-Rum, using singular elsewhere.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r7.speaker: الكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r7.claim: Al-Kisa'i follows Hamza's wind readings, adding the plural at al-Hijr 15:22.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r8.claim: The plural stresses that each wind independently signifies divine unity and benefit; the singular refers to the wind as a genus.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r9.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p168/r9.claim: The Prophet's Companions praised God for continually changing creation: alternating day and night, weather, and other signs show that creation has a Lord who changes it, just as He will replace this world with the next.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r1.speaker: القائلون بأن الخلق غير المخلوق
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r1.claim: They argue that God is called Creator before creating; equating creation with creatures would make Him characterized by devils and filth.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r2.speaker: القائلون بأن الخلق غير المخلوق
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r2.claim: A created thing's arising is rightly explained by God's creating it, but not by its creating itself; therefore creation differs from existence.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r3.speaker: القائلون بأن الخلق غير المخلوق
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r3.claim: Knowing an act and God's power without knowing which power effects it shows that causal efficacy differs from both power and effect.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r4.speaker: النحاة
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r4.claim: In “God created the world,” the world is the object of the verb, not its verbal noun, so the act differs from its object.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r5.speaker: القائلون بأن الخلق غير المخلوق
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r5.claim: The single concept of creating applies to unlike substances and accidents, so it is distinct from each created essence.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم
RAZI-FULL:v4p161#2/r6.claim: The Arabic root of creation means measuring or proportioning; it names God's acts because they are all correctly ordered.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r1.claim: The verse introduces eight kinds of evidence for God's existence and, secondarily, His unity and freedom from partners.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r2.speaker: عالم من الناس
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r2.claim: One position identifies creation with the created object, since the verse's signs occur in created things.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r3.speaker: عالم من الناس
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r3.claim: If the act of bringing something from nonexistence were eternal, it would combine eternal existence with being preceded by nonexistence.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r4.speaker: عالم من الناس
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r4.claim: If the act of creation were originated and distinct from its effect, it would need another act to bring it into existence, causing an infinite regress.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r5.speaker: عالم من الناس
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r5.claim: An eternal God either originates an event, which is then the created thing, or originates nothing, which would mean He never created anything.

RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r6.speaker: عالم من الناس
RAZI-FULL:v4p161/r6.claim: If causal efficacy is originated it entails regress; if eternal, its effect would follow necessarily, making God compelled rather than a freely acting creator.

RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r1.claim: The verse requires rational inference to the Creator's existence; imitation alone cannot achieve that end.

RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r2.speaker: عطاء
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r2.claim: On the Prophet's arrival in Medina, revelation of God's oneness prompted Quraysh to ask how one God could suffice for people; this verse followed.

RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r3.speaker: سعيد بن مسروق
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r3.claim: Quraysh asked Jews and Christians about Moses' and Jesus' signs, then requested a golden Safa for certainty; the verse points to creation as a greater sign.

RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p162/r4.claim: Al-Abhari's study of the heavens through the Almagest illustrates that deeper inquiry into creation brings deeper knowledge of God's majesty.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r1.claim: Observation supports nine spheres, but the text neither affirms nor denies any additional spheres beyond what observation establishes.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r2.speaker: ابن سينا
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r2.claim: Avicenna says he cannot determine whether the fixed stars occupy one sphere or several concentric spheres.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r3.claim: Apparently similar stellar motions may differ by amounts too small to detect over human lifetimes, so their equality is unproved.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r4.claim: Even if motions match, different things can share one property; the argument cannot establish one sphere for the stars or any other celestial sphere.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r5.claim: The observed change in the obliquity of the ecliptic was used to posit an intermediate sphere whose poles shift between the outer and fixed-star spheres.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163#2/r6.claim: A second rationale for an intermediate sphere was disagreement among astronomers over whether the Sun's motion takes equal or unequal times.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r1.claim: The traditional order places the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, fixed stars, then the outermost sphere.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r2.claim: Occultations and planetary colors can identify which body passes in front: the Moon covers planets and stars, Mercury Venus, and Venus Mars; this places the Moon below the Sun.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r3.claim: Parallax is observable for the Moon, Mercury, and Venus, imperceptible for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and tiny for the Sun, placing the Sun between the groups; al-Biruni says only lunar parallax is perceptible.

RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r4.speaker: بطليموس
RAZI-FULL:v4p163/r4.claim: Because Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars can range far from the Sun while Mercury and Venus stay within a small elongation, the Sun lies between the groups; al-Razi objects that the Moon ranges freely yet lies below all.

RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r1.speaker: من يجعل أوج الشمس متحركا
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r1.claim: One explanation of the Sun's irregular motion makes its apogee move, changing the time between the equinoxes according to their distance from the apogee.

RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r2.speaker: أهل الهند والصين وبابل
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r2.claim: Indian, Chinese, Babylonian, and other ancient scholars attribute the variation to shifting of the zodiac sphere and its poles; Hipparchus and talisman-makers reportedly held this view.

RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r3.speaker: بطليموس
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r3.claim: Ptolemy measured fixed-star motion at one degree per century, while later observers found one and a half; al-Razi says the difference implies changing obliquity and another sphere.

RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r4.speaker: القائلون
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r4.claim: They infer a fixed-star sphere above the seven planets because stars move more slowly and those planets occult them.

RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p164/r5.claim: The inference is not demonstrative: planetary motion need not require spheres, the model already has slow deferents, and unocculted polar stars could occupy other locations.

RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r1.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r1.claim: The standard account gives the outermost sphere a rapid daily westward rotation and the eighth, fixed-star sphere a very slow eastward motion.

RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r2.claim: The apparent slow reverse drift can instead result if both spheres rotate westward daily, with the eighth sphere lagging by about ten arcseconds per day.

RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r3.claim: Opposite simultaneous motions would make one body move in two directions, while suppressing its own motion would interrupt the continuous celestial motions assumed by astronomers.

RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r4.claim: A hierarchy of speed fits distance from the outer sphere: the nearer fixed stars move faster, while the farther Moon is slower and the Earth is at rest.

RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p165/r5.claim: The standard astronomical foundations are weak, and reason alone cannot reach certainty about these celestial principles.

RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r1.claim: In the model, the Sun's sphere is divided into an Earth-centered deferent and an eccentric sphere touching it at apogee and perigee.

RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r2.claim: The upper planets and Venus each have two solar-like spheres plus an eccentric carrier sphere containing an epicycle.

RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r3.claim: Mercury's four-sphere scheme adds a displaced director and carrier; the Moon has a great and inclined sphere, with the inclined sphere divided into three.

RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p166#2/r4.claim: Each sphere moves continuously around its center, and the whole construction follows only if the astronomers' starting premises are sound.

RAZI-FULL:v4p166/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p166/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p166/r1.claim: Astronomers rely on two conjectural premises: celestial motions are uniform and continuous, and planets move only through the motion of their spheres.

RAZI-FULL:v4p166/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p166/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p166/r2.claim: Given those premises, apparent changes in a planet's distance, size, speed, and direction require either an epicycle or an eccentric sphere.

RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r1.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r1.claim: Most spheres move eastward, while the outermost sphere and certain Sun, Mercury, and Moon spheres move westward; the outermost carries all bodies through a daily first motion.

RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r2.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r2.claim: The fixed stars make a slow second motion eastward, moving the apsides relative to the zodiac as their poles circle the world's poles.

RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p167/r3.claim: The text gives five reasons for calling the stars fixed: slow motion, planets moving toward them, constant latitude, constant relative spacing and figures, and their use in reckoning time.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r1.claim: Tiny undetected differences over tens of thousands of years mean that similar observed fixed-star motions do not establish equal motions.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r2.claim: Even equal motions would not prove the stars share one sphere; the same uncertainty applies to all spheres, including the daily-moving one.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#2/r3.claim: Changes in measured obliquity and uncertainty about the Sun's timing were offered as grounds for an additional sphere between the outermost and fixed-star spheres.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r1.speaker: من يجعل أوج الشمس متحركا
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r1.claim: One account explains unequal solar motion by a moving apogee, which changes the Sun's distance from the equinoxes.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r2.speaker: أهل الهند والصين وبابل
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r2.claim: Ancient Indian, Chinese, Babylonian, Roman, Egyptian, and Syrian scholars explained the variation through shifting of the zodiac sphere; Hipparchus and talisman-makers reportedly agreed.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r3.speaker: بطليموس
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r3.claim: Ptolemy's one degree per century versus later observers' one and a half degree rate is too large for instrument error and, al-Razi says, implies an intermediate sphere.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r4.speaker: القائلون
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r4.claim: They place fixed stars in a sphere beyond the seven planets because the planets move faster and occult those stars.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#3/r5.claim: This is not proof: celestial bodies need not move only with spheres, fixed stars could occupy slow deferents, and unocculted polar stars could lie elsewhere.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r1.speaker: الجمهور
