RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r1.claim: The usual account gives the outermost sphere a rapid daily westward turn and the eighth sphere a slow eastward turn.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r2.claim: Both spheres may turn westward daily, with the eighth lagging slightly; accumulated tiny differences create the appearance of fixed stars drifting backward.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r3.claim: Opposite simultaneous motions would put one thing in two places at once; denying the eighth sphere's own motion would break continuous celestial motion.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r4.claim: The more distant a sphere is from the outermost one, the slower it moves, down to the Moon and the stationary Earth.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#4/r5.claim: The standard accounts of celestial principles are unsound and cannot be settled by reason.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#5/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#5/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#5/r1.claim: The astronomers' assumptions of uniform continuous celestial motion and planets carried by spheres are conjectural.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#5/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#5/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#5/r2.claim: On those assumptions, apparent changes in planetary distance, size, speed, and direction are explained by epicycles or eccentric spheres.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r1.claim: The Sun's model uses an Earth-centered sphere and an eccentric sphere touching at the apogee and perigee.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r2.claim: The upper planets and Venus use two solar-like spheres plus an eccentric carrier with an epicycle.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r3.claim: Mercury and the Moon have four-sphere arrangements: Mercury adds director, carrier, and epicycle spheres; the Moon's inclined sphere is divided into three.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#6/r4.claim: All these spheres are said to move continuously around their centers, but the construction rests on the disputed premises.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r1.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r1.claim: Most spheres move eastward; the outermost daily rotation moves all celestial bodies and produces their rising and setting.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r2.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r2.claim: The fixed stars move eastward slowly around the zodiac poles, shifting the apsides in the second motion.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#7/r3.claim: Five explanations for “fixed” are their slowness, the planets' approach to them, their stable latitudes and spacing, and their role in calendrical timekeeping.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r1.claim: The source lists daily rates for the centers of eccentric spheres and separate rates for epicycle centers, calling these mean and specific motion.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r2.claim: Four combinations of lunar epicycle and eccentric positions give distances of about 33, 43, 54, and 64 Earth radii; al-Biruni explains the intermediate cases.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r3.claim: Superior planets are at conjunction near apogee and opposition near perigee; the unusually large Martian epicycle can reverse which event places it farther from the Sun.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r4.claim: Venus and Mercury's epicycle centers stay aligned with the Sun; their farthest elongations occur midway between conjunction and opposition.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168#8/r5.claim: Lunar conjunction and opposition occur at its farthest distance, while quadrature with the Sun occurs at its nearest.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r1.claim: The text distinguishes daily mean motion of sphere centers from the planets' specific or anomalistic motion, and lists rates for each.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r2.claim: The Moon's four combinations of position on its epicycle and eccentric sphere yield distances of about 33, 43, 54, and 64 Earth radii; al-Biruni explains the intermediate cases.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r3.claim: Superior planets are in solar conjunction near their apogees and opposition near perigee; Mars's large epicycle can make its conjunction farther from the Sun.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r4.claim: Venus and Mercury's epicycle centers remain aligned with the Sun; their maximum elongations occur midway between conjunction and opposition.

RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p168/r5.claim: For the Moon, conjunction and opposition occur at the farthest distance, while quadrature occurs at the nearest distance.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r1.claim: After an eccentric sphere is removed, its two complementary parts have arbitrarily unequal thickness, requiring a choosing agent.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r2.claim: The spheres move in different directions although all directions are equivalent to them, which requires a governor.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r3.claim: Celestial motion cannot be eternal because motion implies succession; whether the spheres existed still or were absent before moving, their beginning requires an ancient mover. Al-Razi calls this his strongest proof.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r4.claim: Motion is not essential to the particular bodies because they can be conceived apart from each part of their motion; an external mover is required.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169#2/r5.claim: The ordered heavens cannot be chance or purposeless; even if living stars moved themselves, their need for perfection or purposelessness entails a wise sovereign mover.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r1.claim: Each sphere's particular size is contingent despite the possibility of slightly greater or smaller dimensions, so a determiner must specify it.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r2.claim: The mutually touching spheres could occupy different high or low positions because their natures are alike; their particular locations require a determiner.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r3.claim: A planet occupies one side of its sphere although all sides are equal, so this placement also requires specification.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r4.claim: The choice of each sphere's two poles and of its equator from equally possible points and circles requires a determiner.

RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p169/r5.claim: The spheres have distinct speeds despite the intuition that a larger orbit should turn more slowly; their assigned motions therefore require a determiner.

RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r1.claim: Their varied colors, brightness, sizes, compositions, astrological qualities, conjunctions, and motions despite shared purity show that each body's traits were specified by a determiner.

RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r2.claim: If the stars' influences conflict, cooperate, or alternate between the two, each scenario shows that they are not independent governors and need a creator who subdues them.

RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p170/r3.claim: Every body is composite and contingent; its cause is needed at origination or while it remains, while causing an already existing thing anew is impossible, proving a Creator.

RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r1.claim: Bodies share corporeality across their divisions, while each body's contingent size, position, shape, and qualities require an eternal creator to specify them.

RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r2.claim: At the equator, the celestial equator bisects daily circles; night and day do not differ for stars, every non-polar point rises and sets, and the ecliptic and Sun pass overhead twice yearly.

RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p171/r3.claim: At northern and southern latitudes the pole elevation changes, daily paths are divided unequally, and seasonal day and night lengths reverse between hemispheres; some stars become permanently visible or hidden.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r1.claim: The equator divides Earth into northern and southern halves; the inhabited land is said to occupy one northern quarter, while three quarters are said to be water, with the caveat God knows best.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r2.claim: The inhabited world's length is nearly half the Earth's circumference by common agreement, but scholars disagree whether its western starting point is the encircling ocean coast or the Fortunate Islands.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r3.claim: Most place the inhabited breadth no farther than 66 degrees north; Ptolemy also posits habitation 16 degrees south, yielding about 82 degrees total.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172#2/r4.claim: Geographers divide inhabited land into seven longitudinal climates, starting at the equator or around 13 degrees north and ending near 50 degrees, beyond which settlement is sparse.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r1.claim: When pole elevation equals the ecliptic's greatest obliquity, the ecliptic passes overhead, but the Sun does so only at the summer solstice.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r2.claim: At still higher latitude neither the ecliptic nor Sun passes overhead, and the ecliptic's northern pole is always visible while its southern pole is always hidden.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r3.claim: When pole elevation equals the complementary obliquity, the solstitial points only touch the horizon; the ecliptic aligns with it and day or night disappears at the respective solstice.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r4.claim: Beyond that latitude, portions around the summer solstice stay visible and those around the winter solstice stay hidden; reversed zodiacal risings and settings can occur.

RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p172/r5.claim: At the pole the celestial equator lies on the horizon, rising and setting cease, and half the year is day and half night.

RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r1.claim: Earth's varied terrain—land and sea, plains and mountains, rock and sand, hollows and heights—produces sharply differing conditions; he previously treated it under 2:22.

RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r2.claim: Earth is convex in longitude: a flat surface would experience simultaneous sunrise and sunset, contrary to differing eclipse times and elapsed night in eastern and western towns; a concave surface predicts the opposite time relation.

RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r3.claim: A lenticular rather than spherical longitudinal shape is rejected because eclipse durations vary across locations around a circle; thus Earth is spherical in longitude.

RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p173/r4.claim: A flat or concave latitudinal surface conflicts with the changing pole altitude and visibility of circumpolar stars as a traveler moves south; Razi calls this persuasive reasoning.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r1.claim: Earth's conditions more readily prove a creator than the heavens: terrestrial bodies visibly change their places and qualities, so their contingent specification requires an eternal, knowing director.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r2.claim: He says the first reported interpretation of night-day difference is their succession, each replacing the one that has gone.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174#2/r3.claim: A second reported interpretation is variation in night and day length, light and darkness, and increase and decrease.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r1.claim: A lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow; since the eclipsed portion is circular and the shadow follows the light-dark boundary, Earth is round from every side.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r2.claim: Because all parts of Earth seek distance from the celestial sphere in the same way, Razi argues that Earth must be spherical.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r3.claim: Critics object that a centered spherical Earth should be surrounded by water seeking the center, and that its mountains and deep hollows contradict roundness.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r4.claim: The water objection is answered by divine providence exposing land like an island, or water flowing into low places and leaving some ground uncovered.

RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p174/r5.claim: Mountains and hollows are too small relative to Earth to overturn its spherical form, as small irregularities do not stop a wooden ball remaining round.

RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r1.claim: Razi adds a third meaning: night and day also differ by location, so one instant is dawn in one longitude, noon elsewhere, and evening or night elsewhere; latitude changes seasonal lengths too.

RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r2.claim: Night-day conditions point to a creator through eight signs: solar motion, seasons, daily work and rest, mutual benefit despite opposition, sleep and waking as a reminder of resurrection, dawn's advance through darkness, habitable moderate durations, and the Sun's special light-producing role.

RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r3.claim: The gradual dawn breaking through darkness resembles a clear stream running through a turbid sea without either clouding the other; he links this image to the Quranic description of God splitting dawn.

RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r4.claim: A temperate allocation of night and day permits life; near the pole, six months each of day and night would prevent ripening, habitation, and livelihood.

RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p175/r5.claim: If God creates air-light at sunrise by habit, that needs no further argument; if the Sun itself causes it, the Sun's unique efficacy among equal bodies proves a maker.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r1.claim: The Indian Ocean extends from the Ethiopian coast toward India and China, with four named gulfs, measured lengths and widths, and the Arabian lands between the Gulf of Aqaba and Persian Gulf.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r2.claim: The account lists 1,370 inhabited or uninhabited Indian Ocean islands; Serendib is large, mountainous, river-rich, and produces red ruby, while other islands supply tin and camphor.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p176#2/r3.claim: The Maghrib Ocean connects with the Indian Ocean; its far limits are unknown except to the west and north, ships sail near shore, and its account names the Fortunate Islands and a northern gulf toward Bulgaria.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r1.claim: The objection that a huge powerful angel could move the heavens fails for Razi because human capacity cannot originate acts of creation.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r2.speaker: أبو هاشم
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r2.claim: On the Mu'tazilite position, Abu Hashim dismisses the possibility that an angel moves the heavens by transmitted evidence.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r3.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r3.claim: Al-Wahidi derives falak from rotation: it can mean anything round, the seven heavens' orbits, a girl's rounded breast, a spindle whorl, or a ship that turns easily on water.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r4.speaker: سيبويه
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r4.claim: Sibawayh says falak is masculine when singular and feminine when plural; its matching written vowel differs in grammatical meaning, as in his examples for singular and plural nouns.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r5.speaker: الليث
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r5.claim: Al-Layth says the sea is named for its vast breadth, and the verb can describe becoming extensive in knowledge or wealth.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r6.claim: Another etymology derives sea from a split or incision in the earth, the same root as bahira.

RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r7.speaker: الجبائي
RAZI-FULL:v4p176/r7.claim: Al-Jubba'i and other authorities on seas enumerate five major seas: Indian, Maghrib, Rum, Nitas, and Jurjan.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r1.claim: The account gives lengths, widths, gulfs, and island counts for the Mediterranean, the Nitas/Black Sea, and the Jurjan/Caspian Sea; Jurjan does not connect to another sea.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r2.speaker: أرسطاطاليس
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r2.claim: Aristotle is cited as saying the Ocean surrounds Earth like a belt.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r3.claim: Ships depend on God-given materials and tools for construction, and on suitable winds for movement and safety; human beings cannot create or reverse the wind.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r4.claim: God strengthens sailors' hearts to complete voyages and makes ships a means of livelihood, trade, and benefit to both shippers and recipients.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r5.claim: God apportions different goods among world regions and makes each region need others, prompting people to undertake dangerous voyages for mutual gain.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r6.claim: The sea is subdued to carry ships even though its power becomes frightening when storms and winds churn it.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r7.claim: Great rivers continually empty into the small Khwarazm lake without increasing or overflowing it, a water balance whose mechanism God knows.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r8.claim: God protects ships from the sea's immense animals and brings them safely to shore.

RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p177/r9.claim: The meeting of fresh and salt waters without mixing is another sign of God's governance, linked to two Quranic passages.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r1.claim: The phrase that ships run for people's benefit implies permission to sail, earn through trade, and enjoy lawful pleasures.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r2.claim: Rainwater's substance and its thinness, moisture, and sweetness are God's creation; no one else can create it.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r3.claim: Water gives humans life and many benefits, and is the basis of every living thing, as other verses state.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r4.claim: Rainwater also supplies livelihood, in keeping with the statement that provision is in heaven.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r5.claim: Clouds suspend immense quantities of water in the air, which he treats as a great sign.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r6.claim: Rain arrives when creatures plead and need it, in a measured amount beneficial to them; he links this to Noah's call to seek forgiveness.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r7.claim: Other verses describe rain bringing life and growth to dead or barren land, reinforcing the sign.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r8.claim: The objection asks whether rain descends literally from heaven, comes from clouds, or follows a natural account of evaporation and condensation.

RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p178/r9.claim: One proposed natural account says the Sun heats Earth, vapors rise, cool and thicken, then join into raindrops.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r1.claim: Whether animals arise by direct generation or by reproduction, their coming to be requires a wise maker; Razi begins by establishing this for humans.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r2.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r2.claim: In an anecdote, Umar says countless chess games on a small board rarely repeat, but the far greater variety of human faces on a face-sized area is more astonishing evidence of power and wisdom.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r3.claim: A formative power in semen would need knowledge and skill beyond even the fully developed human, who cannot alter a single hair; an unconscious natural power would produce uniform effects, not a structured human.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r4.claim: The complex anatomy and arrangement of animal bodies provide further evidence, though their many marvels cannot be surveyed here.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r5.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r5.claim: Ali is reported to praise the One who gives sight through fat, hearing through bone, and speech through flesh.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179#2/r6.claim: The body's elemental arrangement reverses the theorists' expected hierarchy: earth-like skull bone is uppermost, then water-like brain, air-like breath, and fire-like heart.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r1.claim: Earth's life after death includes vegetation that feeds livestock, crops that feed people, provision for animals, useful colors, tastes, scents, and materials for clothing, as well as the land's renewed beauty.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r2.claim: Calling land alive or dead is metaphorical: only a perceiving, knowing subject literally lives or dies, while vegetation brings beauty, freshness, growth, and flourishing.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r3.claim: The creator is evident in crops that no human can produce in their form, their countless colors and tastes, and their regular appearance at appointed times.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r4.claim: Razi affirms that water descends from heaven as revelation says; if God can hold it in clouds, holding it in heaven is equally possible.

RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p179/r5.claim: Water from the seas on Earth is possible, but cannot be asserted decisively without denying a freely choosing creator and affirming an eternal world, which Razi calls unbelief.

RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r1.claim: Human creation uniquely combines all four elements in ways other makers avoid, as the Quran describes Adam from earth, life from water, spirit from breath, and jinn from fire.

RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r2.claim: A child cannot survive when its mouth and nose are blocked after birth, yet lives without breathing in the womb; its initially weak understanding later grows into the strongest animal intelligence, showing divine gift rather than nature.

RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p180/r3.claim: Human languages, temperaments, constitutions, and appearances vary greatly, while wild and mountain animals resemble one another; human diversity preserves livelihood by preventing confusion of persons.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r1.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r1.claim: Al-Wahidi explains the syntax of wa-taṣrīf al-riyāḥ as an understood verbal noun with the object expressed by the genitive construction, a common usage.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r10.speaker: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r10.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed that a blowing wind be made plural winds rather than a singular wind, associating the plural with mercy.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r11.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r11.claim: The Quran often uses plural winds for glad tidings of mercy and singular wind for the sterile punishment sent against Ad; Quranic phrasing can mark a specialized sense.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r12.claim: He adds that Quranic expressions such as what will make you know about the Hour signal an unspecified matter, unlike expressions that explain what the subject is.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r2.speaker: أبو علي
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r2.claim: Abu Ali says the singular rīḥ is a feminine form whose original wāw becomes yāʾ through the kasra; the few plural is arwāḥ, while the many plural riyāḥ has a kasra-driven change like dīma/diyam and ḥīla/ḥiyal.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r3.speaker: ابن الأنباري
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r3.claim: Ibn al-Anbari derives rīḥ from rūḥ because winds usually bring spirit and relief, whereas stillness brings distress; arwāḥ confirms the original wāw.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r4.claim: The four winds are north, south, eastward ṣabā, and westward dabūr; ṣabā is called qabūl because it faces dabūr, and intermediate directions are crosswinds.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r5.claim: Abu Amr, Asim, and Ibn Amir read the word in the plural in ten locations, including this verse.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r6.speaker: نافع
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r6.claim: Nafi reads the plural in twelve locations, adding Ibrahim 14:18 and al-Shura 42:33 to the ten listed places.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r7.speaker: ابن كثير
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r7.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the plural in five locations: al-Baqara, al-Hijr, al-Kahf, and two places in al-Rum.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r8.speaker: الكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r8.claim: Al-Kisa'i reads the plural in three locations: al-Hijr, al-Furqan, and the first al-Rum occurrence.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p181#2/r9.claim: Singular rīḥ can mean the generic wind, so singular and plural readings can convey the same sign; the cited prophetic supplication prefers plural wording for mercy-bearing winds.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r1.claim: Air is created in a form that can be moved, then directed to benefit people, animals, and plants; its ubiquity reflects how vital it is, while rarer needs become progressively harder to obtain.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r2.speaker: الشاعر
RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r2.claim: An unnamed poet expresses that God makes scarce goods costly though people may do without them, and makes air easy to obtain although every breathing creature needs it.

RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p181/r3.claim: Winds drive ships, and no human or collection of humans can turn a north wind south or move still air at will.

RAZI-FULL:v4p182/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p182/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p182/r1.claim: Clouds are named for gliding through air, and their subjugation has three signs: heavy water stays aloft, their measured amount avoids both overcast harm and drought, and God steers them by winds where He wills.

RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r1.claim: The plural signs may refer either to all the listed phenomena together or to each phenomenon individually; each of the eight has many indications of a creator.

RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r2.claim: Each sign points to many divine attributes: its coming-to-be indicates power, order indicates knowledge, occurrence at a chosen time indicates will, and coherence without corruption indicates oneness, as 21:22 says.

RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r3.claim: For those who hold that reason establishes a duty to thank the benefactor, abundant blessings also prove that people owe God sincere gratitude.

RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v4p183/r4.claim: Even indivisible parts of these vast bodies have contingent size, time, and qualities, so every part testifies to dependence on the described creator; all created things thereby praise God in effect.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r1.claim: Clouds are suspended and carried like birds; 16:79 and 67:19 say God alone holds birds in the sky.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r2.speaker: كعب الأحبار
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r2.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar says clouds sieve rain, preventing it from damaging the earth; he also says seed descends from heaven, as transmitted through Ibn Abbas.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r3.claim: The listed phenomena are signs of God's unity and power, deliberately following the declaration that God is one and displaying mercy toward creation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r4.claim: A prophetic warning says woe to someone who recites this verse and then fails to reflect or draw a lesson.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r5.claim: The world cannot create itself: a nonexistent thing cannot be living, knowing, powerful, and willing, while an existent thing needs no self-creation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#10/r6.claim: If self-creation were possible, buildings, carpentry, and weaving could create themselves; since that is impossible, the implication is impossible.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r1.claim: Qur'an 10:101 addresses disbelievers, 7:185 calls them to inspect signs in the heavens and earth, and 51:21 directs them to examine themselves.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r2.claim: Reflection on change shows that the cosmos is originated and needs a maker; that maker must be wise, knowing, powerful, willing, hearing, seeing, and speaking, or a human would surpass him.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r3.claim: Human development from drop to embryo and flesh, and from youth to old age, happens without self-direction; this proves a maker transfers people between states.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#11/r4.claim: A philosopher says each feature of the macrocosm has a counterpart in the human microcosm, connecting 95:4 with the call to inspect oneself in 51:21.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r1.claim: The senses correspond to the stars, hearing and sight to sun and moon; the body also contains analogues of earth, water, air, and fire.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r2.claim: Veins are rivers, the liver the springs feeding them, and the bladder a sea receiving the body's fluids.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r3.claim: Bones resemble mountains, organs trees, and body hair the plants and grasses of the earth.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#12/r4.claim: Humans can imitate animal sounds and movements, making the person a small world alongside the large world, both created by one maker.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r1.claim: A poem about two kinds of tharid uses layl and nahr, illustrating the vocabulary for night and daytime.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r10.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r10.claim: Adi used white and black cords to distinguish day from night; the Prophet replied that his pillow was broad, meaning night-darkness and day-whiteness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r11.claim: This dawn-based definition governs oaths: someone who swore not to speak by day breaks the oath by speaking before sunrise; the Prophet's wording decides the dispute.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r12.claim: A language-and-Sunna-based view takes day to begin once broad daylight appears; the passage cites a poem for this interpretation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r2.speaker: ابن فارس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r2.claim: Ibn Faris lists nahr and anhar as plurals of nahar and defines day as daylight from dawn to sunset.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r3.speaker: النضر بن شميل
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r3.claim: Al-Nadr says day begins at sunrise, excluding the time before it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r4.speaker: ثعلب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r4.claim: Thalab also says Arabs begin the day at sunrise and adduces Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's sunrise poem.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r5.speaker: عدي بن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r5.claim: Adi ibn Zayd's verse marks the sun as separating day from night, supporting a sunrise-to-sunset day.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r6.speaker: الكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r6.claim: Al-Kisa'i's poem likewise associates daytime with the sun's rising.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r7.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines the beginning of day as the sun's appearing.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r8.speaker: ابن الأنباري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r8.claim: Ibn al-Anbari divides time into night from sunset to dawn, day from sunrise to sunset, and an interval shared by both from dawn to sunrise.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#2/r9.claim: Qurtubi holds that day runs from dawn to sunset, citing Ibn Faris and Adi ibn Hatim's report in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet interprets the cords as night-darkness and day-whiteness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r1.claim: A poem cited for the broad-daylight definition describes a hand breaking open an opening, with something visible beyond it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r2.speaker: حذيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r2.claim: A report from Hudhayfa, transmitted by al-Nasa'i, supports the broad-daylight view; fasting passages will return to the question.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r3.claim: Fulk means ships; singular and plural share the form but differ in vocalization, and the dual fulkan shows a separate plural pattern.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r4.claim: The Qur'an uses fulk as masculine in 36:41 and feminine here, and as a plural in 10:22; it can denote one vessel or several.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r5.claim: Some derive fulk from rotation, as in the sky's orbit, a girl's rounded breast, and a spindle whorl; a ship is so named for turning easily in water.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r6.claim: The ship is a sign because God makes it run over water and remain afloat despite its weight.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r7.claim: Noah first built ships after Gabriel showed him how, as reported; Ibn al-Arabi likens the vessel to an inverted bird, water below and air above.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#3/r8.claim: This verse and comparable passages establish that sea travel is generally permissible for trade or worship, including pilgrimage and jihad.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r1.claim: The Prophet was asked about sea travel when water was scarce; this report and Anas's Umm Haram account support sailing for jihad by men and women.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r2.claim: If sailing for jihad is permitted, sailing for obligatory pilgrimage is even more warranted; the Anas report has variant attribution through Umm Haram.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r3.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r3.claim: Umar ibn al-Khattab and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz are reported to have prohibited sea travel, a view Qurtubi says Qur'an and Sunna refute.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r4.claim: The prohibition reports can be read as caution against risking lives for worldly gain, not as a ban on fulfilling religious duties.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r5.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r5.claim: Ibn al-Arabi reasons that God placed people on opposite shores and divided benefits between them, so ships ease the necessary crossing of the sea.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r6.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r6.claim: Malik disliked women sailing for pilgrimage and jihad; Basran associates explain this by small Hijazi ships, lack of privacy, crowding, and an available land route, unlike larger Basran ships.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r7.speaker: أبو عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r7.claim: Abu Umar states the principle that pilgrimage is obligatory for any free adult who can reach it by a generally safe route, regardless of sex or sea versus land.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r8.claim: Qur'an, Sunna, and reason permit sailing for worship and trade, but a person unable to bear it or perform required prayer must not sail.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#4/r9.claim: Sailing is forbidden when the sea is storm-tossed or safety is generally unlikely; permission applies when survival is more likely.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r1.claim: What benefits people in ships includes trade and other needs that improve their circumstances; both merchants and recipients of goods benefit.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r2.claim: In reply to a critic asking where spices are mentioned despite the Qur'an saying nothing is omitted, Qurtubi points to the phrase about what benefits people.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r3.claim: Rain revives the world and brings forth plants and provision; God also stores some water underground for later use, as 23:18 says.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r4.claim: Batha means dispersed and spread, as in the phrase about scattered moths; dabbah covers all animals, including birds that walk on their legs.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r5.speaker: الأعشى
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r5.claim: Al-A'sha's phrase about the step of desert pigeons illustrates that birds are included among creatures that move on foot.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r6.speaker: علقمة بن عبدة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r6.claim: Alqama ibn Abdah likewise uses dabib of birds, supporting their inclusion under dabbah.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r7.claim: Winds vary as barren or fertilizing, calm or stormy, destructive or helpful, hot or cold; they also differ in direction and are regulated to carry ships safely.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r8.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#5/r8.claim: The Prophet forbade cursing the wind because it brings mercy and punishment, and taught people to ask God for its good and seek refuge from its harm.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r1.speaker: ابن ماجه
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r1.claim: Ibn Majah transmits a version repeating the ban on cursing wind and the prayer for its good and protection from its evil.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r2.claim: A variant calls wind the nafas of the Merciful; Qurtubi explains this as relief, refreshment, and release attributed to God as its maker.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r3.claim: The Prophet said he was aided by the east wind and the people of Ad were destroyed by the west wind; Qurtubi links this to the wind at the Confederates.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r4.claim: Nafasa means to relieve distress, as in the cited hadith about God relieving a Muslim's distress and a poem about the east wind easing grief.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r5.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r5.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi says nasim is the first breath of wind.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r6.claim: The root of rih is rawh, so the small plural is arwah; riyah is a larger plural for euphonic agreement, and Hafsa's codex reads arwah.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r7.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#6/r7.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read rih singular here and in several passages; the other named qira'a variants continue in the next segment.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r1.claim: The seven readers agree on the plural reading in the phrase al-riyah mubashshirat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر يزيد بن القعقاع
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r2.claim: Abu Ja'far generally reads winds in the plural when the definite article is present, with two exceptions; without the article he uses the singular.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r3.claim: Singular reading can denote generic wind in both small and large amounts; plural can reflect winds arriving from different directions.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r4.claim: Plural is commonly paired with mercy and singular with punishment, following the Qur'an's dominant pattern; Yunus 10:22 is an exception for a single steady ship-driving wind.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r5.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed for winds in the plural rather than a singular wind; Qurtubi explains mercy winds as gentle and broken up, punishment wind as compact and severe.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#7/r6.claim: Wind is moving air; a wind from the qibla-facing side toward the qibla is called saba.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r1.claim: The four cardinal winds have distinct directions and temperaments: east hot-dry, west cold-moist, south hot-moist, and north cold-dry.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r2.claim: The four seasons follow these air qualities: spring is warm and moist for growth, summer hot and dry for ripening, autumn cold and dry for harvest, and winter cold and moist before spring renews growth.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r3.claim: Many other winds exist, but the four are foundational; a wind between two is called nakba and takes its ruling from the nearer direction.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#8/r4.claim: Sahab is named for gliding through air; musakhkhar most plainly means moved from place to place, though another view says it stays suspended unsupported.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r1.claim: The Prophet described a cloud directed to water a named man's garden; its water collected in a channel, and the gardener said he gave a third in charity, kept a third for family, and reinvested a third.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r2.claim: Qur'an 35:9 and 7:57 describe winds raising clouds and carrying them to a dead land, among many similar passages.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r3.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r3.claim: When a threatening cloud approached, the Prophet sought refuge from its harm, prayed for beneficial rain if it rained, and praised God if it passed without rain; Ibn Majah transmits the account.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r4.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r4.claim: A Muslim report says the Prophet looked anxious in wind and cloud because he feared punishment for his community, then called rain mercy and recalled the people of Ad mistaking a cloud for rain.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164#9/r5.claim: These reports and verses show that subduing clouds means moving them, not merely keeping them suspended; being between heaven and earth remains true, and their carriage is a greater sign.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r1.speaker: عطاء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r1.claim: After the declaration that God is one, Quraysh asked how one deity could suffice all people; the verse was revealed in response.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r10.claim: Layl has the collective plural layl as with tamra/tamr and nakhla/nakhl, and also the exceptional plurals layali and layal.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r11.claim: Layali and similar plurals depart from regular patterns; the poetry cites laylat, and Ibn Faris reports an uncertain bird-name layl.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r12.speaker: ابن فارس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r12.claim: Ibn Faris says a certain bird is reportedly called layl, though he does not know the bird.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r13.speaker: أحمد بن يحيى ثعلب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r13.claim: Thalab treats nahr as a plural of nahar, itself a collective plural for day; another view treats nahar as a singular verbal noun meaning illumination, with the plural view more common.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r14.claim: The source cites poetry using laylat and nahr and notes nahar may be an unpluralized singular like diya, applying to little or much.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r2.speaker: أبو الضحى
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r2.claim: A report through Sufyan says Quraysh asked for proof of the one God, and this verse supplied signs of divine unity.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r3.claim: The world's remarkable construction requires a builder and maker, so its order evidences God's oneness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r4.claim: The heavens are plural because they comprise differing kinds, while earth is singular because it is all soil.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r5.claim: The heavens' height without supports below or attachments above manifests power and the breaking of ordinary patterns.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r6.claim: A prophet's stopping a mountain in the air without support would count as a miracle, by analogy with the unsupported heavens.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r7.claim: The sun, moon, moving stars, and bright planets, whether rising, setting, shining, or eclipsed, are further signs.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r8.claim: The earth's seas, rivers, minerals, trees, plains, and rugged places are signs of divine power.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:164/r9.claim: Night and day differ by one arriving as the other departs in a way people do not know how to cause, or by light and darkness and changing lengths.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164#2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164#2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164#2/r1.claim: If two gods' wills agree, a shared effect entails two efficient causes for one effect, while action by only one entails preference without a cause and incapacitates the other; if they differ, they contend and thwart one another.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164#2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164#2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164#2/r2.claim: The verse thus points to the distinction of theology and its practitioners and urges investigation and rational inquiry.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r1.claim: The heavens are plural because they are distinct layers differing in essence, while the earth is singular because earthly layers are not so distinct.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r10.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r10.claim: A prophetic warning says woe to the person who recites this verse without pondering it.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r11.claim: The contingent heavens and earth could have taken many different forms and motions; their specific ordering therefore requires a wise, powerful creator acting by will.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r2.claim: The alternation of night and day means their succession, as in the description of them as following one another.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r3.claim: The ships signify the sea and its marvels; they are singled out because they prompt voyaging and discovery, and mentioned before rain and clouds because these usually originate in the sea.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r4.claim: Fulk is feminine because it means a ship; it is also read with two dammas either in its original form or as a plural, whose damma differs from the singular.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r5.claim: The first min marks origin and the second explains the water; al-sama may mean the celestial sphere, clouds, or the direction above.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r6.claim: The earth is revived by plants; the phrase about creatures attaches either to the sending of rain and resulting life or to revival, since creatures grow in fertility and live through life.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r7.claim: Bāth means spreading and dispersing; tasrif al-riyah means directing winds through different paths and conditions, and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the noun in the singular.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r8.claim: The restrained cloud neither descends nor disperses, despite natural forces tending toward either, until God's command; another view says God directs winds to turn it through the air.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:164/r9.claim: These signs benefit people who reflect and look with the eyes of reason.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r1.claim: The verse answers polytheists astonished by one God and demanding a sign: created phenomena provide the proof they requested.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r2.claim: Night and day differ in color, length, and shortness, and alternate in departing and returning.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r3.claim: Ships carry what benefits people, or benefit people through what they transport.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r4.claim: Rain descends from the sky, revives the earth after its dryness, and God disperses every creeping creature through it.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r5.claim: The word min marks origin with sky and species with water; it may also be partitive because rain is the first portion of what descends.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r6.speaker: حمزة وعلى
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r6.claim: They read الريح in the singular; winds turn among directions and conditions, including hot, cold, stormy, gentle, barren, pollinating, merciful, and punitive.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r7.claim: Clouds are subdued to God's will and rain wherever He wishes; rational reflection infers the Creator's power, wisdom, and oneness.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p82#2/r8.claim: A prophetic report warns of woe for reciting this verse without reflection or taking heed.

QASHANI:2:164/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:164/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:164/r1.claim: The heavens, earth, alternation of light and darkness, and the body's ship signify spirit, heart, intellect, soul, and the body's pursuit of human perfection.

QASHANI:2:164/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:164/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:164/r2.claim: Knowledge descends from the spirit like water and revives the soul from ignorance; animal faculties live through the heart.

QASHANI:2:164/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:164/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:164/r3.claim: Changing winds signify increasing divine acts and clouds signify divine attributes; these are signs for reason illuminated by revealed law and free from illusion.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p61/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p61/r10.speaker: ابن فارس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p61/r10.claim: Ibn Fāris says layl is also the name of a bird, reportedly the young of the bustard.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p61/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p61/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p61/r9.claim: Although some treat layl as a collective like tamr, Abū Ḥayyān says it is singular and has no attested plural; layālī is plural of laylah.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r1.claim: Nahār has regular plurals nahr and anhura; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the claim that it is an unpluralizable verbal noun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r2.claim: The Prophet told ʿAdī that the fast’s white thread is the brightness of day and its black thread the darkness of night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r3.claim: The apparent linguistic boundary of daytime begins with dawn and ends at sunset.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r4.speaker: النضر بن شميل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r4.claim: Al-Naḍr says daytime begins at sunrise, excluding the preceding period.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r5.speaker: الزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r5.claim: Al-Zajjāj places the start of daytime at the sun’s first appearance, adducing Umayyah’s verse about sunrise before dawn’s final night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r6.speaker: ابن الأنباري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r6.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says daytime runs from sunrise to sunset, while dawn until sunrise belongs jointly to night and day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p62/r7.claim: Fulk is a shared form for singular and plural with the same vowel pattern; singular can be dualized as fulkān and is masculine, while feminine agreement can reflect plural use.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r1.claim: Baṯṯ means to spread, disperse, and make manifest; poetry depicts a snake and scorpion spread through the land.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r2.claim: Dābbah covers every animal; ʿAlqamah’s image of birds’ movement answers those who exclude birds. Its feminine ending may be literal or intensive, and it applies to either sex.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r3.claim: Taṣrīf is the verbal noun of ṣarafa, whose sense is turning or sending something back.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls ʿUmārah’s use of ariyāḥ in poetry ungrammatical.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r5.speaker: أبو حاتم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r5.claim: Abū Ḥātim also says ariyāḥ is impermissible, though ʿUmārah challenged him with the familiar form riyāḥ.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r6.claim: Abū Ḥayyān recalls attested classical poetry using ariyāḥ, formed from the singular despite the sound-change cause disappearing in the plural, as in ʿīd/aʿyād.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r7.speaker: أبو علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r7.claim: Abū ʿAlī derives saḥāb from withdrawal and also reports ḥabā, crawling, as another name for clouds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r8.speaker: الراغب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p63/r8.claim: Al-Rāghib defines taskhīr as coercing something into action, stronger than mere compulsion; Abū Ḥayyān first glosses it as subjection and making something compliant.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r6.claim: After 2:163, Quraysh reportedly asked how one God could suffice all people, so this verse was revealed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r7.claim: After asserting oneness and exclusive divinity, God presents wondrous creation as evidence from effect to agent and craft to maker, teaching people where to look and how to reason.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p76/r8.claim: Creation may mean bringing the heavens and earth into existence, or composing and arranging their bodies and parts, as in describing someone’s fine form.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r1.claim: The suggestion that khalq is redundant and the verse simply means “in the heavens and earth” is weak: Arabic does not establish redundant nouns, and creation arises from will rather than being will itself.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r2.claim: The heavens are plural because they are distinct kinds, while earth is singular because all of it is soil; heaven is mentioned first for its rank, scale, and contents.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r3.claim: Among the heavens’ signs are their unsupported height, celestial bodies and their cycles, and their immense scale; astronomers give measurements for the sun, stars, and seven spheres.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p77/r4.claim: Abū Ḥayyān cites as sound the Prophet’s report that heaven groans, with no space of a foot lacking a prostrating angel.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r1.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r1.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says Gabriel told Noah to set the ship on a bird’s chest, making the ship an inverted bird with water below like air above.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r2.claim: The ship’s sign is God’s subjection of it to float, stay above water despite its weight, and carry people to their destinations; a thrown stone would sink.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r3.claim: The relative clause highlights the ships’ continual renewed sailing; naming the sea reinforces their setting, and attributing motion to ships is figurative.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r4.claim: If mā is relative, ships travel carrying useful goods, with bāʾ indicating accompaniment; if it is a verbal noun, they benefit people’s trade and journeys, with bāʾ indicating cause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r5.claim: The verse mentions benefit rather than harm because the ships are presented as a divine favor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r6.claim: The two min phrases in the rain clause may mark origin and then apposition, genus, or part; the second min phrase can attach to the verb despite the first min having a different sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78#2/r7.claim: The fa links sending rain to the earth’s quick revival; revival and death are metaphors for visible plant growth and what remains dormant within the earth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r1.claim: Earth’s signs include its unsupported spread, waters, mountains, trees, terrain, minerals, and the different benefits and harms suited to each region.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r2.speaker: أرباب الهيئة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r2.claim: Astronomers describe earth as a point inside a circle, encircled by seas, air, fire, and the celestial spheres.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r3.speaker: الباقلاني
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r3.claim: Al-Bāqillānī records disagreements among earlier thinkers about whether earth is stationary or moving, alongside varied speculative theories of the heavens.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r4.claim: Astronomical models rest on rational inference, not revelation; only God knows the created reality unless He discloses it by revelation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r5.claim: Night and day may alternate by one succeeding the other, by light and darkness, or by length and shortness; Ibn Kaysān also says they may be equal.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r6.claim: One view places night first because it was created first, citing the night stripped of day; another says light preceded darkness, affecting which night counts as the night of a given day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r7.claim: These competing definitions also affect legal interpretation of an oath not to speak during daytime.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r8.claim: Noah was the first to build a ship.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p78/r9.claim: Abū Ḥayyān continues a sound Prophetic report: the Inhabited House receives seventy thousand visitors each day, who never return before Resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r1.claim: Connecting “and He spread” to the preceding relative clauses requires a deleted return pronoun, but the grammatical conditions for deleting this prepositional pronoun are absent.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī proposes connecting the phrase either to “sent down” or to “revived”; Abū Ḥayyān says both still require the missing pronoun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r3.claim: Abū Ḥayyān supplies an omitted relative, reading “and what He spread in it of every creature,” as a separate sign of the remarkable forms, traits, movements, uses, and designs of land and sea creatures.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p79/r4.claim: Deleting a relative pronoun when context makes it understood is common in Arabic according to some grammarians, though Basrans do not accept it by analogy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p80/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p80/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p80/r1.claim: Poetry supplies examples of omitting a relative pronoun: an unnamed poet omits the complement after “on whom,” and another line by Ḥassān omits “who praises him.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p80/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p80/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p80/r2.claim: The Quran also omits a relative in “and He sent down to you,” understood as “and what He sent down to you,” matching another verse’s “the Book sent down to His Messenger.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r1.claim: Readers distribute singular and plural forms among Quranic passages: Ḥamzah has singular exceptions at al-Furqān, al-Kisāʾī at al-Ḥijr, and other readers have their own exceptions.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r10.claim: Clouds are “subjugated” by holding heavy water aloft, delivering a measured amount where needed, withdrawing it afterward, or moving by winds; each account indicates divine oneness.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r2.claim: Ḥafṣ’s codex reads “spirits” here; the reciters agree on singular when the word has no definite article.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r3.claim: The cited recitations vary between singular and plural forms, with readers following different distributions across the passages.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r4.claim: The Quran generally uses plural winds with mercy and singular wind with punishment, except the pleasant wind in Jonah; where the noun is indefinite, readers agree on the singular.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r5.claim: Abū Ḥayyān cites a supplication asking that winds be plural rather than singular; no transmitter or grading is given.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r6.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says punishment wind is a single joined mass, while gentle mercy winds are dispersed; wind is singular for ships’ connected parts and disambiguated by “good.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r7.claim: A singular reading may denote the generic and so convey the same sense as the plural.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r8.claim: The syntax permits “winds” to be nominative with taṣrīf annexed to its agent, or accusative with the source semantically annexed to its agent, meaning God directs the winds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r9.speaker: كعب الأحبار
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p81/r9.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār calls clouds a sieve for rain, saying rain would ruin the earth without them; others say clouds draw rain from sky or earthly seas, or that God creates it within them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r1.claim: “Between heaven and earth” is adverbial, governed either by “subjugated” or by an understood “being”; the emphatic lām enters because the predicate intervenes after inna.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r2.claim: The phrase “for people” qualifies the signs; only rational people infer from these wonders God’s oneness, sole divinity, power, and wisdom.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r3.claim: An unnamed transmitted warning says woe to whoever recites the verse without digesting it, meaning without reflecting and taking heed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r4.claim: The verse follows the oneness assertion by offering signs and blessings that prompt reflection, though they benefit only those able to reason with God-given intellect.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r5.claim: There are eight signs, or nine if “He spread” begins a separate omitted-relative clause; they reduce to four categories: creation, alternation, rain, and direction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p82/r6.claim: Creation comes first as the greatest proof of divinity because it brings something forth from absolute nonexistence and implies God’s essential attributes.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p83/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p83/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p83/r1.claim: The sequence moves from heavenly creation to effects of celestial bodies, then ships associated with earthly bodies, then shared rain and growth, and ends with winds and clouds that complete the preceding benefits.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p83/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p83/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p83/r2.claim: The signs fall into what intellect apprehends and what the eyes observe; reason traces visible signs back to the necessary existent, so the verse says “for people who reason,” not “who see.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p95/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p95/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p95/r5.claim: The signs begin with the invention of the upper heavens and dense earth, and the alternation of night and day through the motions God placed in the upper cosmos.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p95/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
