ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p95/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p95/r6.claim: Ships move back and forth for human benefit through what God placed in the lower world; rain, the earth's revival, and animal life join the upper and lower realms.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p96/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p96/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p96/r1.claim: Winds and clouds between heaven and earth complete the blessings that sustain marine and terrestrial human interests.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p96/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p96/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p96/r2.claim: These cosmic signs guide rational people to God's oneness and exclusive divinity; idols cannot produce any of them and, like all creatures, depend on God and change.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p413/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p413/r5.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p413/r5.claim: Al-Razi says this passage gives six signs rather than al-Baqara's eight, omitting ships and clouds because wind governs their motion; here the signs form three groups.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r1.claim: Al-fulk coordinates with the genitive khalaq governed by fī, not with al-samāwāt in an iḍāfa.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r10.claim: In bi-mā yanfaʿ, mā may be a relative noun and bi marks accompaniment, or a particle with bi marking cause: ships sail for people's benefit in trade and other things.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r11.claim: On the second parsing, mā is a particle and bi expresses the cause of sailing, namely people's benefit through trade and other uses.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r2.claim: Fulk can be singular, as in Q 26:119, or plural, as in Q 10:22.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r3.speaker: سيبويه
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r3.claim: For plural fulk, Sībawayh's preferred account is a broken plural whose vowel change is only estimated; the author calls this correct.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r4.claim: Sībawayh infers that fulk is not a shared singular/plural form because speakers form its dual fulkān, unlike shared-form junb and shalal; hījān and dilāṣ show how vowel patterns may differ by number.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r5.speaker: الأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r5.claim: Al-Akhfash analyzes plural fulk as a collective noun, like ṣaḥb and rakb.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r6.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r6.claim: The Shaykh regards fulk as shared by singular and plural; the author rejects this on the evidence of its dual form and notes no rationale was offered.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r7.claim: When singular, fulk is masculine; feminine agreement in the verse does not prove feminine singular usage because the word may be plural.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r8.claim: Fulk derives from rotation, as in the celestial sphere and a spindle whorl; the verb describes a girl's breast becoming rounded.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#2/r9.claim: The present verb tajrī conveys ongoing renewal; attributing running to ships is figurative, and 'in the sea' is explanatory emphasis, like 'flies with its wings' in Q 6:38.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r1.claim: The first min in min al-samāʾ marks origin; the second may explain the material, mark partitive selection, or with its phrase serve as an appositive to min al-samāʾ, repeating its governor.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r2.claim: Both prepositional phrases attach to anzala; two identical prepositions may share a governor when their meanings differ or when the second phrase is an appositive.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r3.claim: The restriction against two same-form prepositions under one governor applies only when they share meaning without coordination or apposition; the verse avoids that problem.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#3/r4.claim: Alternatively, the first min can modify an omitted circumstantial expression for the relative mā itself or for the object pronoun in anzalahu: what God sent down while it was from heaven.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r1.claim: Fa-aḥyā coordinates with anzala and its immediate-result fāʾ signals rapid growth; bi-hi may mark cause or instrument, figuratively, and the pronoun refers to the relative mā.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r2.claim: Batha most clearly coordinates with anzala inside the relative clause; because aḥyā already coordinates with anzala, the two verbs together function as one unit.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the clause means God sent water into the earth and spread creatures there, which grow through fertility and live through life-giving abundance.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r4.claim: An alternative attaches batha to aḥyā, but the Shaykh objects that this relative clause then lacks a linking pronoun unless one is supplied as bi-hi.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r5.claim: Deleting a prepositional pronoun is normally allowed only under stated matching, attachment, nonrestriction, and linking conditions; those conditions fail here because the relative is not governed by the same preposition.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r6.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r6.claim: To avoid the missing-link problem, the Shaykh proposes deleting a nominal relative pronoun, a common construction he says the Basrans disallow, and cites poetry and Q 29:46 and 4:136.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r7.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#4/r7.claim: The Shaykh also allows the first analysis despite the missing-pronoun condition, adducing poetic examples with an understood prepositional complement.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r1.claim: Min kulli dābbah has three parses: kull is batha's object with partitive min; min is extra per al-Akhfash and kull the object; or the phrase is a circumstantial complement of an omitted object after a deleted relative, with min explanatory or partitive.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ posits an omitted object such as 'creatures of every kind'; the author finds this unhelpful because it makes min kulli dābbah merely its adjective.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r3.claim: Bath is spreading and dispersal; its present is normally yabuṯṯu, though the kasra form is also attested for doubled transitive verbs, as in namma al-ḥadīth.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r4.claim: Dābbah denotes any animal, including birds; the restriction excluding birds is refuted by verses from ʿAlqama and al-Aʿshā and by Q 24:45, which then divides creatures by their modes of walking.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r5.claim: ʿAlqama's simile describes birds as moving with a creeping gait, showing that birds count as dābbah.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#5/r6.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line compares the movement of partridges to creeping, further supporting inclusion of birds among dābbah.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r1.claim: Taṣrīf means turning and alternation; its iḍāfa may make the winds the agent and omit the object (clouds), or make them the object and omit the agent (God).

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r2.claim: Riyāḥ is a broken plural whose yāʾ comes from wāw in rīḥ; phonological conditions convert wāw to yāʾ, but it returns in arwāḥ when those conditions are absent.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r3.claim: Two cited poetic lines use arwāḥ, evidencing the restored wāw in the plural of rīḥ.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r4.claim: Abū Ḥātim corrected ʿUmārah b. ʿUqayl's poetic al-aryāḥ as impermissible; the poet accepted the correction after citing riyāḥ.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r5.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r5.claim: The Shaykh recalls that al-aryāḥ occurs in poetry by authoritative Arabs, apparently modeled on the singular despite the missing sound-change trigger, like ʿīd/ aʿyād.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r6.claim: The author supports retaining yāʾ in al-aryāḥ to distinguish winds from arwāḥ, just as aʿyād distinguishes feast-days from sticks (aʿwād); the diminutive is also ʿuyayd.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r7.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says the Qurʾān usually uses the plural with mercy and singular with punishment, with an exception at Q 10:22; a report asks God for winds in plural, not a singular wind.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#6/r8.claim: The author rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's formulation because readings vary at eleven places; more precisely, no plural occurs with punishment, while singular occurs with both, explaining the prophetic preference for plural in the supplication.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r1.claim: At this locus Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read al-rīḥ singular, while the rest read plural: plural signals kinds such as southerly, westerly, and easterly winds; singular means the generic kind.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r2.speaker: أبو علي
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r2.claim: Cloud (saḥāb) is a collective noun with singular saḥābah; Abū ʿAlī derives it from sliding or gliding, like ḥabī from crawling.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r3.claim: As a collective noun, saḥāb takes masculine singular agreement in al-musakhkhar (Q 54:20), plural agreement in Q 7:57, and can take feminine singular agreement in Q 69:7; collective nouns allow agreement by form or meaning.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r4.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#7/r4.claim: Taskhīr is subduing an object and making it obedient; al-Rāghib says compelling it to act is stronger than coercion.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#8/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#8/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#8/r1.claim: Bayna al-samāʾ can be governed by al-musakhkhar as the location of subjection, or be a circumstantial phrase from the passive participle's hidden pronoun, with an omitted 'being'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164#8/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#8/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164#8/r2.claim: Li-āyāt is the predicate of inna placed before its delayed subject; the lām marks that postponement, and li-qawmin is an adjectival phrase for āyāt while yaʿqilūn is an adjective clause for qawm.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r1.claim: Layl is a singular with no attested plural; layālī is plural of layla, though some analogize it as a plural of layl or posit an underlying layāh.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r10.claim: Ikhtilāf is a verbal noun whose genitive is its agent: night and day each succeeds the other, as in Q 25:62 and the cited poetry.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r11.claim: Zuhayr's line uses khalfa for alternating succession, with gazelles and their young following one another.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r12.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r12.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r12.claim: Night precedes day in the verse because it comes first; Q 36:37 supports this ordering, which the author calls the sounder view.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r13.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r13.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r13.claim: The alternative says light precedes darkness; on that view the night belongs to the preceding day, whereas on the preferred view it belongs to the following day, affecting how the Day of ʿArafa is classified.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r2.claim: The verse of poetry attests layl as a singular, while the diminutive layīla supports the analysis; layālī is an unusual plural like kayka/kayāk.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r3.claim: The verse glosses layālī through a poet's form laylāh; the source leaves the poet unnamed.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r4.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r4.claim: In legal usage, nahār runs from dawnbreak until sunset.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r5.claim: The apparent lexical sense starts at the first lightening of dawn; Thaʿlab and al-Naḍr instead define day as beginning at sunrise, and al-Naḍr excludes the earlier time.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r6.speaker: الزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r6.claim: Al-Zajjāj locates the start of day at the sun's spreading light.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r7.claim: Nahār has plurals nahr and anhura, supported by usage and verse; the reported view that it has no plural treats it as a verbal noun, but the author affirms the plurals.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r8.claim: A cited line contrasts a night meal with a day meal and witnesses nahr as a form for daytime.

SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:164/r9.claim: The root of nahār denotes breadth or expansion, reflected in the expanse of daylight and Q 2:25.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r1.claim: The heavens are vast, elevated and adorned with moving and fixed stars and revolving spheres; earth is dense, low, and filled with varied terrain, settlement, and benefits.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r10.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r10.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r10.claim: These phenomena plainly demonstrate God's oneness and invite rational reflection, as the passage about thoughtful remembrance also says.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r2.claim: Night and day succeed one another without delay; their lengths vary and each can gain time from the other.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r3.claim: Ships cross the sea by God's subjection of it, carrying people's livelihoods and goods between regions.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r4.claim: Rain revives dead earth, as another passage illustrates through crops, gardens, springs, and fruits.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r5.claim: God spreads creatures of differing forms, colors, uses, and sizes, knows them all, and provides for them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r6.claim: Winds alternate between mercy and punishment, herald clouds, drive, gather, scatter, and redirect them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r7.claim: Wind names and directions are related to how they pass the Kaaba: southern, Yemen-facing, eastern ṣabā, and western dabūr.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r8.claim: Many books discuss the languages and rules of winds, rain, and stellar weather signs, but their detailed treatment is lengthy here.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p474#2/r9.claim: Clouds travel between heaven and earth under God's control, directed to whichever lands and places He wills.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r1.claim: Quraysh asked Muhammad to make al-Ṣafā gold so they could buy horses and weapons, believe, and fight with him; after their pledge, he declined the threatened punishment and asked time to invite them gradually.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r2.claim: A second transmission adds the challenge that Quraysh could already see signs greater than turning al-Ṣafā to gold.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r3.speaker: عطاء
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r3.claim: After 2:163 was revealed in Medina, Quraysh in Mecca asked how one God could suffice for everyone; this verse's signs taught them that He is the one Lord and creator of all.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r4.speaker: أبو الضحى
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r4.claim: When the polytheists demanded a sign after hearing that God is one, this verse's signs were revealed in response.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p475/r5.claim: The signs in creation teach that God is one, the deity of everything and creator of everything.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p293/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p293/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p293/r3.claim: The signs in 2:164 expand the preceding evidence to prove God's knowledge and power and, especially, exclusive divinity, since apparent proximate causes do not act independently.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p294/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p294/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p294/r1.claim: The final community was spared the demand for extraordinary signs because earlier peoples who denied them were punished; the Prophet's sign is revelation, so this community is invited to learn through created evidence instead.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p294/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p294/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p294/r2.claim: The rhetorical ellipsis mentions creation first as evidence for omitting it second, then mentions variation second as evidence for omitting it first.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r1.claim: The ordered union of opposites, such as fire with water and air with earth, cannot be produced by creatures; their combination in bodies and organs shows the one God whose effects are visible and whose reality reason can recognize.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r2.claim: Large ships are distinguished from small boats; their sailing is figuratively attributed to them although only God makes them move, rejecting philosophers' belief in the independent agency of stars.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r3.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r3.claim: The ships distribute useful goods among peoples and directions; the general phrase 'what benefits people' includes every useful cargo and points to human cooperation.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p295/r4.claim: Rain from the sky revives the barren earth after its lack of growth, and the water disperses every kind of self-moving creature across it.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r1.claim: Al-Harali says God's name is made manifest with the earth where life is visible, while his name is shown where it is hidden from people; water's arrival draws worship toward the God above.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r2.claim: The Prophet tested a slave woman's faith by asking where God is; she answered 'in heaven,' and he told her owner to free her.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r3.claim: Wind changes direction under divine governance, while clouds are suspended between heaven and earth despite their weight and contrary to the tendencies of dense and subtle matter.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r4.claim: The visible elements also signify inner realities: rain revives hearts with knowledge, and winds and clouds portray the changes between a servant's outward and inward life under God's rule.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r5.claim: The 'people' who understand are those mature in strong reflection, and reason is a divine light by which they read the signs in creation and scripture.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p296/r6.claim: The variations show a freely acting, powerful creator who can resurrect the dead and is one without rival; they also encompass the essential beliefs about God's existence, unity, transcendence, creation, and governance.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p298/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p298/r1.speaker: البيهقي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p298/r1.claim: Al-Bayhaqi says that the divine names established by scripture and scholarly agreement are distributed among the five essential beliefs, and a name may belong to more than one category.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p298/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p298/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p298/r2.claim: Proofs are multiplied because capacities differ: sensory knowledge of the visible world is open to everyone, while the unseen is grasped by people of sound intellect; creation offers varied routes proportionate to each person's capacity except for sealed hearts.

DURR-FULL:v1p395/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r1.claim: An account says Quraysh asked for the Ṣafā to be made gold; God offered it with a warning of unmatched punishment if they disbelieved, and the Prophet deferred them while pointing to greater cosmic signs.

DURR-FULL:v1p395/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r2.claim: Quraysh asked about Moses’ signs, then requested a golden Ṣafā; the verse was revealed to show creation of heaven and earth is a greater sign.

DURR-FULL:v1p395/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r3.speaker: أبو الضحى
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r3.claim: After polytheists challenged the claim that God is one and demanded a sign, this verse was revealed, declaring these signs evidence for people who reason.

DURR-FULL:v1p395/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r4.speaker: عطاء
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r4.claim: When Meccan Quraysh questioned how one deity could suffice for people, the signs in this verse showed that God is one and creator of everything.

DURR-FULL:v1p395/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r5.speaker: سلمان
DURR-FULL:v1p395/r5.claim: A report describes night and day as initiated by angels lowering black and white jewels, with sunset and sunrise occurring when the sun sees them.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r1.speaker: أبي بن كعب
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r1.claim: When wind rises, one should ask God for its good and the good it carries, and seek refuge from its harm.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن شداد بن الهاد
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r2.claim: Wind is from God’s spirit; when it appears, ask for its good and seek refuge in God from its harm.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r3.speaker: عبدة
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r3.claim: Some winds bring mercy and others punishment, so one should ask that they be winds of mercy.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r4.claim: Water and wind are among God’s armies, and wind is the greatest of His armies.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r5.claim: Wind has two wings and a tail.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r6.speaker: ابن عمرو
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r6.claim: One account divides eight winds into four merciful winds—spreading, announcing, sent, and scattering—and four punitive winds, two on land and two at sea.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r7.claim: A second list also counts eight winds, naming the merciful winds as spreading, announcing, sent, and gentle, and the punitive as barren, violent, storming, and crushing.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r8.speaker: عيسى ابن أبي عيسى الخياط
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r8.claim: A report counts seven winds and gives their names and directions: east, west, south, north, intermediate crosswinds, and the breath of creatures.

DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r9.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v1p396#2/r9.claim: The four main winds can be oriented by facing the Kaaba’s door: north lies to the left, south to the right, east ahead, and west behind.

DURR-FULL:v1p396/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r2.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r2.claim: The phrase about spreading every kind of creature means God spread created beings through the earth.

DURR-FULL:v1p396/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r3.speaker: جابر
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r3.claim: The Prophet advised limiting outings once night becomes quiet, since God spreads whatever creatures He wills at night.

DURR-FULL:v1p396/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r4.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r4.claim: Winds may be merciful pollinators and bearers of clouds, or a barren, non-pollinating punishment wind.

DURR-FULL:v1p396/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r5.speaker: أبي بن كعب
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r5.claim: In the Qur’an, plural winds signify mercy, while the singular wind signifies punishment.

DURR-FULL:v1p396/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r6.speaker: أبي بن كعب
DURR-FULL:v1p396/r6.claim: The Prophet forbade cursing the wind, calling it a breath of the Merciful.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r1.claim: When people cursed a wind, Ibn Abbas told them not to: it brings both mercy and punishment, so ask God to make it merciful.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r2.speaker: عمر
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r2.claim: When a strong wind swirled, Umar would call for takbīr, saying it was a remover.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r3.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r3.claim: The Prophet forbade cursing night, day, sun, moon, or wind, since each may bring punishment to some and mercy to others.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r4.speaker: كعب
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r4.claim: Kaʿb called clouds a sieve for rain: without them, falling water would ruin the ground; he also said seeds descend with rain and the earth alternates what it grows.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r6.speaker: خالد بن معدان
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r6.claim: Clouds grow as fruit on a tree in Paradise; ripe black fruit bears rain and unripe white fruit does not.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r7.claim: A report says the earth asked not to receive water in torrents as at the Flood, and God promised a cloud to sieve it.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r8.speaker: الغفاري
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r8.claim: The Prophet described clouds forming as speaking and laughing beautifully.

DURR-FULL:v1p399/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r9.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p399/r9.claim: A report says that when a sea-originating cloud mass forms and converges, it signals a heavy rain.

BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r1.claim: The heavens and earth are created with marvels that human minds cannot fully comprehend; the heavens are plural because they differ in kind or have separate orbits, while earths share the substance of soil.

BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r2.speaker: ابن التمجيد
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r2.claim: In the philosophers' account, each heaven's convex surface touches the concave surface above it, except the ninth sphere; authorities disagree whether the space above it is void.

BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r3.claim: Night and day alternate, each following the other, and vary in length, darkness, and light.

BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r4.claim: Ships stay afloat despite their weight and the water's lightness, and move back and forth with a single wind; الفلك is a collective singular with feminine agreement.

BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r5.claim: The ships carry useful goods: merchants profit from transport, and recipients benefit from what arrives.

BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#2/r6.claim: The rain's origin is the direction above; 'heaven' can mean the celestial sphere or anything elevated, including clouds, and the phrase introduces water as a type.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r1.claim: Rain revives the land with plants, flowers, and trees; its death is the loss of crops and leaves as dryness takes hold.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r10.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAmr counts eight winds: four bring mercy, while the barren and violent winds bring punishment on land or sea.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r11.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r11.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r11.claim: Clouds are a divinely governed kind that moves quickly through the air; the noun is singular though treated collectively, and can be understood by singular or plural agreement.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r2.speaker: ابن الشيخ
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r2.claim: The land's new beauty and growth are likened to an animal's life because both bring freshness, splendor, and increase.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r3.claim: Creatures are spread across the land after rain revives it, since fertility and rain sustain their growth and life.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r4.claim: Wind rotation includes changes in direction, warmth, force, and effects; another reported interpretation distinguishes winds of mercy from winds of punishment.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas calls wind and water God's greatest armies and links the name الريح to its refreshing effect on people.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r6.speaker: وكيع الجراح
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r6.claim: Wakiʿ says that without wind and flies the world would become foul-smelling.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r7.speaker: شريح القاضي
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r7.claim: Shurayh says each wind either heals someone ill or makes someone healthy ill.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r8.speaker: بكر بن عباس
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r8.claim: Bakr says the four winds prepare every cloud drop: the east wind stirs it, the south gathers it, the west fertilizes it, and the north disperses it.

BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p215#3/r9.claim: The four primary winds come from the cardinal directions; winds between their bearings are called nakbāʾ because they veer from the primary courses.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p216/r1.claim: The cloud's suspension itself is wondrous: if light it should rise, and if dense it should fall.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p216/r2.claim: The indefinite plural 'signs' magnifies their number and greatness; the delayed predicate permits the emphatic lām, and rational observers read these signs with minds and hearts.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p216/r3.claim: People who reflect on these phenomena infer God's immense power and wisdom, recognize Him as creator, and affirm His oneness.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p216/r4.claim: The verse rebukes polytheists who demanded a confirming sign: these changes already suffice, so their failure to recognize them shows poor judgment.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p216/r5.claim: The Prophet warns that woe awaits whoever recites this verse without taking it to heart; the author explains the image as failing to consider it.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p216/r6.claim: The source ranks the declaration of divine oneness as the first level of tawhid from God's side, while humans begin with oneness of acts and are guided through attributes toward oneness of essence.

BURSEVI:v1p216/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p216/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p216/r7.claim: The source attributes the staged descent from tawhid of essence through attributes to acts, with creation as evidence, to al-Taʾwīlāt al-Qāshāniyya.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r1.speaker: أبو الضحى
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r1.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits an interrupted report that the Quraysh had 360 idols around the Kaaba; on hearing the verse they demanded a recognizable proof, and it was revealed in response.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r2.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the polytheists' extreme ignorance kept them from accepting the comprehensive proof already implied by the verse's two descriptions.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r3.claim: The heavens are plural because people benefit from all their parts, including starlight, whereas the earth is singular because only the one earth they observe benefits them.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r4.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r4.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says earth is not pluralized because the plural is heavy and would oppose the pattern; some singulars have no Qurʾanic plural and some plurals no singular.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r5.speaker: بعض المحققين
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r5.claim: A scholarly view says the seven heavens are distinct personal layers, whether touching as philosophers hold or separated by journeys of five hundred years in reports; differences in their effects indicate different natures.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r6.claim: Night and day may mean their alternation, each succeeding the other, or their internal variation in length, increase and decrease, darkness and light.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r7.claim: Night is mentioned before day either because it was created first or because it is more noble.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r8.claim: The phrase about ships is coordinated either with the creation of the heavens or with night and day, not with the word heavens alone.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p30/r9.claim: Fulk is used for both singular and plural; its vowel may be original as in qufl or incidental as in asad, and the syntax can reveal number.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r1.speaker: الكواشي
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r1.claim: Al-Kawāshī says fulk and fulk with two ḍammas are dialect forms whose written form is the same in singular and plural, distinguished by verb-pronoun agreement.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r2.claim: In bimā yanfaʿu al-nās, mā can be a verbal noun, meaning by their benefiting people, or a relative pronoun, meaning what benefits them; a descriptive mā poorly fits the argument.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r3.claim: The pronoun with the verbal-noun reading may refer to the ship (masculine in form, feminine in meaning), its sailing, or the sea.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r4.claim: The rain clause is coordinated with ships; its later placement despite its broader benefit may give it extra emphasis, while another account explains the ship mention as a route to knowledge of the sea's wonders.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r5.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the proposal that the sea, rather than ships, is the actual object of inference: it reverses the revealed order without evidence, and ships themselves display divine ordering.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r6.claim: Ships can themselves be signs through their changing courses, heavy cargo, and buoyancy amid waves despite the air's delicacy and their own weight; their travel serves human livelihood.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p31/r7.claim: The order first pairs upper and lower creation, then phenomena shaped by heaven and earth, then ships moving in the sea; rain follows as a sign linking the upper and lower worlds and benefiting people.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r1.claim: The night, sun, moon, and ship passages are compared with the signs in another verse; there the night/day signs explicitly mediate between ship and its mention, whereas this verse first hints at them and then turns to rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r10.claim: Winds follow the revived earth and creatures because they nourish plants and preserve animal life; some reports say that if God withheld wind for an hour, everything between heaven and earth would stink.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r2.claim: The two occurrences of min are read first as indicating origin and then as explanatory; min al-samāʾ means the direction above, though other grammatical parses are possible.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r3.claim: God revives the earth by stirring its latent growth and bringing forth plants, flowers, and trees after dryness has suppressed their appearance.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r4.claim: The clause about spreading creatures may coordinate with sending down water as an independent sign sharing God's agency, or with reviving earth as a consequence of the water; on the latter parse, water sustains animals and their spread follows life.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r5.claim: Min kulli dābbah is explanatory of the kinds of creatures that crawl on earth; their multiplication by birth or generation is evidence because every kind is represented, not just some kinds.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r6.claim: A partitive reading is proposed because not every possible individual was created, but al-Ālūsī objects that partitive min denotes a portion of its complement, not one individual of a kind; heavenly creatures do not undermine the earthly reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r7.claim: God's turning of winds includes directions, warm and cold, violent and gentle, barren and fecund, and winds of mercy or punishment.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r8.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r8.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the noun in the singular, with الريح understood generically; Ibn ʿAbbās distinguishes plural winds of mercy from singular wind of punishment.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r9.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ALUSI-FULL:v2p32/r9.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed when wind blew: asking that it be winds of mercy and not a wind of punishment; al-Ālūsī relates this to the cited scriptural usages.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r1.claim: Sahāb is a collective noun, with sahābah as its singular; the name may derive from its drifting through the air or from winds drawing it along.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r10.claim: The verse supports rational proof, the nobility of kalām and its scholars, and perhaps the discipline of astronomy.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r2.claim: Al-musakhkhar is an adjective for cloud, matching its grammatical form or its collective meaning; bayna is an adjunct, or a circumstantial phrase with an omitted complement about winds turning the cloud by God's will.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r3.claim: The cloud's subjection means it neither falls nor vanishes, although its lightness would naturally lift it and its density would make it descend; another parse makes it subject to winds that turn it.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r4.claim: Cloud follows wind because it is like the wind's effect and because ending with a heavenly sign echoes the opening's upper-and-lower ordering.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r5.speaker: بعض الفضلاء
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r5.claim: One scholar says wind and cloud come last despite their natural order to stress that each listed phenomenon is an independent sign; al-Ālūsī doubts that anyone would otherwise mistake them for one sign.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r6.claim: The delayed predicate of inna bears the emphatic lām, and its indefinite form magnifies the signs in both number and greatness: they attest overwhelming power, wisdom, and mercy, warranting exclusive worship.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r7.claim: Yaʿqilūn uses reason figuratively for reflection, the fruit of reason; a report from ʿĀʾishah says the Prophet warned readers who recite the verse without reflecting.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r8.claim: Contingent things take one determinate form among possibilities and entail specific effects, so they require a chooser who is powerful, knowing, and wise; this reasoning also reproaches the polytheists' demand for another sign.

ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v2p33/r9.claim: Two independent gods would either jointly cause one effect, leave one without a reason to be preferred, or oppose each other's different intentions; every case entails incapacity, incompatible with divinity.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r1.claim: By apprehending and applying causality through these routes, reason necessarily recognizes God’s existence, unity, and encompassing mercy from the signs.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r10.claim: Human beings’ partial, relative intuition connects them to the First Intellect and thereby gives them access to truth.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r11.claim: Innate intuition is not acquired by human effort, but each person’s share and the habitual intuitive skill gained through sustained experience are acquired.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r12.claim: God summons all people to reason along this path; miracles that act directly on the senses have little benefit without reason.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r13.claim: The Qur’an guides people toward universal rational truths more than miracles and is itself the greatest miracle.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r14.claim: This emphasis on reason must not be construed as denying prophetic miracles or claiming the Seal of the Prophets showed no physical miracles.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r15.claim: Given the immense ongoing wonders of creation, turning Ṣafā to gold is neither significant nor impossible for divine power.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r16.claim: In its revelation context, the verse says an isolated, temporary wonder is a small request beside the immense, enduring miracles of creation and the benefits of contemplating them.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r17.claim: Those who study creation and follow its laws could eventually pave Ṣafā or even all Meccan mountains with gold by understanding mineral laws; they should seek greater, lasting, sacred aims.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r18.claim: Here signs means clear marks, decisive proofs, and manifest miracles that leave no serious room for objection; Qur’anic verses are called signs in this sense.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r19.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r19.claim: God has active signs in the book of creation and verbal signs in the revealed book; both indicate the divine essence, attributes, rulings, and will.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r2.claim: Reflective thought is reason’s slow, gradual, temporal course; intuition reaches its object immediately in a single swift leap.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r20.claim: The two books and kinds of signs mutually indicate, interpret, and explain one another.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r21.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r21.claim: Perfect knowledge reads creation’s active signs through the revealed book, then recognizes God’s essence and attributes and follows divine laws toward the straight path and abiding in God.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r22.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r22.claim: The concise verse gathers clear evidence that one sustaining Creator orders the varied universe, possesses encompassing power and mercy, suffices for all beings, and has no peer; both ordinary and high intellects can grasp it.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r23.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r23.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r23.claim: The Qur’an takes the roots of the highest scientific aims and makes them clear and simple enough for people of every capacity to understand.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r24.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r24.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r24.claim: People habituated to empty, transient poetic fantasy may fail to feel the Qur’an’s miraculous height because their natural taste and reason have been impoverished by caprice.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r3.claim: One kind of intuition is acquired through prolonged study, experience, and practice; theoretical and practical training cultivate it, and it is also called acquired or received intellect.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r4.claim: The other kind is an innate divine gift, called sacred, natural, or inborn intellect; effort does not produce it, and everyone has some share.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r5.claim: Without innate intellect, acquired intellect has no effect; innate intuition has unbounded ranks, from simple intelligence up to prophetic intellects.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r6.claim: The highest rank, the First Intellect, sees beginning from end and end from beginning with perfect certainty and is identified as the Divine Pen and Muhammadan Light.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r7.claim: Hadith reports cited here say that the first thing God created was the Prophet’s light, the Pen, or the intellect.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r8.claim: Differences in intellect’s degrees arise from deficiencies; fundamentally the path of intellect is one, the path of truth.

ELMALILI:2:164#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164#2/r9.claim: Innate apprehension of first principles such as causality and noncontradiction is a share in the First Intellect’s grasp and evidence of the perfection of absolute sacred power.

ELMALILI:2:164/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r1.speaker: Said b. Mesrûk
ELMALILI:2:164/r1.claim: Quraysh asked Jews and Christians about Moses’ and Jesus’ signs, then asked Muhammad to turn Ṣafā into gold; God warned of punishment if they denied it, but Muhammad asked to continue calling them gradually, so this verse pointed to creation as a greater sign.

ELMALILI:2:164/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r10.claim: Clouds subdued between heaven and earth, along with the other phenomena, are signs and material, spiritual, religious, and worldly blessings more miraculous than the requested sign.

ELMALILI:2:164/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r11.claim: These signs benefit people who reason and actually use their intellect; intellect itself is one of the signs and perhaps the greatest.

ELMALILI:2:164/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r12.claim: Intellect is an immaterial light rooted in heart and soul and radiating in the brain, by which people apprehend what is not sensed.

ELMALILI:2:164/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r13.claim: Reasoning apprehends causal relations between causes and effects, agents and acts, and their necessary connections, then infers from effect to cause, cause to effect, or one effect to another.

ELMALILI:2:164/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r14.claim: Inference can discover an unseen animal from a rustle, honey from a bee, or honey and its location from the buzz of an unseen bee.

ELMALILI:2:164/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r15.claim: Particular-to-particular inference is analogy, also called legal analogy.

ELMALILI:2:164/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r16.claim: Induction moves from particulars to universals; most or all general propositions and scientific rules are discovered this way, making observation and experiment important.

ELMALILI:2:164/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r17.claim: Deduction moves from universal to particular and applies the sciences in practice; it derives practical results from induction and is the strongest scientific method because it both establishes and confirms.

ELMALILI:2:164/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r2.claim: The ordered creation and its ongoing processes are greater, more beneficial, and more compelling miracles than Quraysh’s requested golden Ṣafā.

ELMALILI:2:164/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r3.claim: The heavens comprise countless celestial bodies, vast distances, visible and unseen matter or subtle qualities, paths, orbits, systems, and constellations.

ELMALILI:2:164/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r4.claim: Earth’s seas, lands, mountains, valleys, plains, deserts, springs, rivers, minerals, plants, and forests are linked to the heavens without pillars or girders.

ELMALILI:2:164/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r5.claim: Night and day alternate in succession, lengthen and shorten, and manifest spatial arrangement, time, and opposites recurring in one place.

ELMALILI:2:164/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r6.claim: Ships carry useful cargo across the sea; their motion recalls celestial travel, while the created sea and laws of motion and rest provide human benefits.

ELMALILI:2:164/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r7.claim: Water sent down from above revives dry earth after its death, displaying how plant life is formed.

ELMALILI:2:164/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r8.claim: God classifies and spreads every kind, class, and species of animal across the earth, extending as far as rational beings.

ELMALILI:2:164/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:164/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:164/r9.claim: The changing winds, moved from direction to direction and state to state, are another sign.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r1.claim: The verse follows the declaration of divine oneness as proof for a claim many would deny, supplying clear evidence that observers must accept.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r2.claim: Here إن draws attention to the report; its wording may treat people as deniers of the signs because they fail to act on them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r3.claim: إن does not causally explain the preceding sentence: a causal clause would need to fit a فَ connection, as ʿAbd al-Qāhir explains.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r4.claim: The signs establish God's existence and oneness, answering Quraysh polytheists primarily and also their materialists; their secrets yield insight according to people's reason and learning.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p76/r5.claim: Khalq is a verbal noun encompassing both the created heavens and earth and their integrated arrangement, perhaps the system of the planets and earth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r1.claim: Singular al-samāʾ can mean the visible atmosphere; plural al-samāwāt here means ordered celestial bodies, perhaps the seven heavens, while earth is one world (or its layers when plural elsewhere).

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r2.claim: Al-khalq is singular because it encompasses the total heavens together with earth, with the genitive construction governing both coordinated nouns.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r3.speaker: الفخر
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r3.claim: Fakhr reports that al-Abharī, asked what he and Ibn al-Ḥusām were reading in the Almagest, called it an explanation of how the sky was built; deeper study of creation deepens knowledge of God's majesty.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r4.claim: The celestial system's stability and gravity are signs; the greatest secrets include its spherical form and orderly motion, which never breaks down.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p77/r5.claim: Created things mutually supply one another without being depleted: the sea feeds atmospheric moisture, while rivers and valleys replenish it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r1.claim: Al-fulk is coordinated with khalq and ikhtilāf and governed by fī; the relative clause makes ships a sign by sailing and a blessing through human benefit.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r2.claim: The sea itself is wondrous: it covers most of the globe, contains living things and chemicals, and releases useful particles into the air; sailing on water also shows divinely inspired human ingenuity.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r3.claim: God inspired Noah to make ships among humanity's earliest inventions and made their movement across the sea a sign of human access to an otherwise impassable surface.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r4.claim: Daily coastal winds reverse between morning and evening as sun-warmed land air rises and cooler sea air replaces it; these regular breezes benefit fishers and traders.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p80/r5.claim: Seasonal trade winds reverse twice yearly as the sun shifts between the tropics; they are common off Yemen, Hadramawt, and the Indian Ocean.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r1.claim: Ships benefit people through trade, visiting, warfare, and other activities; the verse generalizes these benefits concisely.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r2.claim: Al-fulk is certainly plural here because many ships are the sign; its singular and plural forms sound alike, though lexicographers give differing vowel patterns.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r3.speaker: ابن الحاجب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r3.claim: Ibn al-Ḥājib treats fulk as grammatically feminine without a feminine suffix, pointing to the Qur'anic phrase al-fulk tajrī.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r4.claim: The author calls the unusual damma reading of the singular weak and rejects al-Kawāshī's claim that both singular and plural have a damma on lām, for lack of linguistic authority.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r5.claim: God's commendation of ships supports travel by sea without necessity, including for raids, pilgrimage, and trade.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r6.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r6.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet told Umm Ḥarām he had seen members of his community raiding by sea as kings on couches; she asked to join them, and he prayed for her.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p81/r7.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra tells of a man asking the Prophet about taking little water aboard while sailing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r1.claim: The rain clause coordinates with the preceding nouns as a relative clause, preserving the passage's paired themes of sign and blessing; naming God's act of sending evokes its causes.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r2.claim: Singular al-samāʾ means the atmosphere surrounding earth, familiar to all listeners.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r3.claim: Rain descending from the sky, although water would ordinarily be expected to spring from earth, is a striking sign.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r4.claim: He proposes that water vapor condenses in a cold upper atmospheric layer as sunlight weakens; upper bodies, especially the moon, may contribute to that cold.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p82#2/r5.claim: An unattributed transmitted report says rain descends from a sea beneath the Throne, understood as water's element originating there and reaching the atmosphere; he also links hail to mountains in the sky.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r1.claim: The fa-clause quickly follows rainfall with earth's revival; both the action and sequencing indicate a sign and a blessing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r2.claim: Calling earth alive is a metaphor from the growth powers of animals; if life literally means growth, the construction is figurative attribution and refers to vegetation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r3.claim: Pairing sky with earth and life with death creates two antitheses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r4.claim: The clause about spreading creatures may coordinate with the rain clause or with reviving earth; each analysis makes it an independent sign and blessing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r5.claim: If coordinated with sending rain, min is explanatory; if with reviving earth, min is partitive and signifies many creatures of every kind.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r6.claim: Bāthth originally means exposing what was hidden, as in airing a grievance or secret; it then metaphorically describes proliferation and general spreading.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r7.speaker: أم زرع
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r7.claim: In the report of Umm Zarʿ, the sixth wife says her husband does not probe her secret; the wording illustrates uncovering hidden matters.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r8.speaker: الحماسي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r8.claim: A Hamāsa poet's line uses mabthūth for something spread through the earth, illustrating the broader sense of baṯṯ.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p83/r9.claim: If coordinated with the rain clause, spreading creatures means creating and multiplying kinds of animals on earth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r1.claim: If wabath is coordinated with reviving earth, it describes creatures spreading into pastures after being weak and crouched and reproducing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r2.speaker: لبيد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r2.claim: Labīd's verses picture rainfall, vegetation rising, and young gazelles and ostriches; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Qur'anic wording is shorter, broader, and more eloquent.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r3.claim: The word dābbah means any creature moving on earth; kull rules out restricting it to quadrupeds and includes every kind.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p84/r4.claim: The revived earth and multiplied creatures outline natural history's three origins—minerals, plants, and animals—and point to astronomy, physics, physical geography, and meteorology.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r1.claim: Wind blowing, becoming still, and changing direction each indicate a wise Creator; winds also relieve heat, bring clouds, repel locusts, and bring birds or other benefits.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r2.claim: Local changes of wind direction bring cooler air after hot, moist air after dry, and help sailors return from voyages or fishing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r3.claim: He explains wind through an atmosphere of nitrogen and oxygen with water vapor, heated by sun and earth; warm, light air rises and denser cold air replaces it, producing movement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p85/r4.claim: Wind is the general motion; a mild movement is a breeze and a rapid, strong movement a whirlwind, with other named kinds as varieties.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r1.claim: Riyāḥ is the broken plural of rīḥ; its wāw changes to yāʾ under kasra, as in dīmah/diyam and ḥīlah/ḥiyal.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r2.claim: The cloud phrase may coordinate with wind-management or with winds, meaning God moves clouds from place to place; its creation, control, and position are signs and blessings.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r3.claim: Clouds form when sea and land vapor meets cold air, condenses into mist, dew, or cloud, and eventually becomes rain; their height lets water penetrate earth and keeps it from suffocating people.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r4.claim: Because seas cover more of the globe, most atmospheric vapor comes from them; people formerly imagined clouds' tendrils drawing all rainwater directly from the sea.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r5.speaker: أبو ذؤيب الهذلي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r5.claim: Abū Dhuʾayb's poem depicts dark clouds that drank sea water before rising, illustrating the old image of rain clouds drawing from the sea.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r6.speaker: البديع الإصطرلابي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p86#2/r6.claim: Al-Badīʿ al-Iṣṭirlābī compares a patron's generosity to the sea receiving rain from clouds made of its own water.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r1.claim: Without winds moving clouds, rain would fall only into seas; clouds bless through their formation, transport, and position until their water becomes heavy and descends.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r2.claim: The plural āyāt fits because each listed feature of creation contains signs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r3.claim: One possible reading is that these signs prove God's existence against Arab materialists, completing the groups named as disbelievers before the return to polytheists in the next verse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r4.claim: He prefers that the signs prove oneness, since proving a creator's existence alone does not require exceptional reason and the argument follows God's declaration of oneness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r5.claim: For polytheists who admit that God creates, the ordered system and its interactions show a single wise, knowing, powerful deity; Ibn ʿĀshūr connects this to the non-creator idols and the argument of mutual hindrance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p87/r6.claim: Another possible audience is nations that assign creation to multiple gods, such as Persian Magians and Greek polytheists; the Naml also uses these signs to deny any god beside God.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p88/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p88/r1.speaker: عمرو بن معدي كرب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p88/r1.claim: The word qawm can mean a group of men, a man's tribe, or a nation; the poet's line illustrates its tribal use.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p88/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p88/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p88/r2.claim: Calling them a people characterized by reason presents reasoning as a settled communal trait and hints that those who ignore the signs lack deeply rooted reason.

TABATABAI:2:163-164/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-164/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-164/r7.claim: The signs in this verse demonstrate the preceding claims that the human community has one God, who is universally merciful and guides toward ultimate happiness.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r1.speaker: المثبتون
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r1.claim: Believers in a creator have long affirmed one or many makers of the whole world; the Qur’an presents monotheism as earlier than idolatry, and Max Müller is cited on the antiquity of belief in a creator.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r2.claim: Theists do not posit God only to fill gaps in knowledge: they hold that the entire connected world, including known natural causal chains, depends on a cause beyond that chain.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r3.claim: He points out the materialists’ inconsistency: they accept determinism for all events, including human actions, yet suppose that human creation could escape dependence on the world's first cause.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r4.speaker: الحكماء الباحثين
TABATABAI:2:163-167#2/r4.claim: Philosophical proofs begin from universal causality and argue that possible causes must ultimately depend on a Necessary Existent; they apply this even where a natural cause is known.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r1.claim: The Qur’an affirms universal causation: it attributes natural events and human choices to their proximate agents, while also attributing every thing to God.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r2.claim: Some verses attribute an act both to its human agent and to God, as with human work and the Prophet’s throwing; this preserves both levels of attribution.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r3.claim: God’s creation of each thing includes delimiting it by material causes and temporal and spatial conditions; the Qur’an repeatedly describes creation as measured.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r4.claim: The Qur’an does not assign only unexplained events to God while leaving explained events solely to material causes; all causation ultimately depends on God.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167#3/r5.claim: He traces these mistaken arguments to a distorted, weak popular theology inherited from medieval church philosophy and other theologians, which denied divine dependence for known causes and human choices.

TABATABAI:2:163-167#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167#4/r1.speaker: بعض المحدثين والمتكلمين
TABATABAI:2:163-167#4/r1.claim: Some hadith scholars, literalist theologians, and others deny that human-made products, especially objects made for sinful uses such as wine and gambling tools, are attributable to God because the Qur’an calls them Satan’s work.

TABATABAI:2:163-167/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167/r1.claim: Ships, like other natural entities, depend on God for existence and governance; the Qur’an calls ships His property and says He subjects them to sail by His command.

TABATABAI:2:163-167/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167/r2.speaker: الماديون
TABATABAI:2:163-167/r2.claim: Materialists argue that belief in a creator arose because early people could not identify material causes; as science explains those events, they expect it eventually to explain spiritual life too and remove the need for a creator.

TABATABAI:2:163-167/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:163-167/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:163-167/r3.claim: He rejects treating human-made things as detached from God merely because human choice produces them; human agency remains dependent on God like natural causes.

TABATABAI:2:164#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r1.claim: “Creating the heavens and earth” includes their diverse structures, forms, materials, transformations, growth and decline; he links these processes to two other Qur’anic passages.

TABATABAI:2:164#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r2.claim: Night–day variation arises from Earth’s daily rotation and the inclination of its equatorial plane relative to its orbital plane, which shifts the Sun north and south and produces seasons.

TABATABAI:2:164#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r3.claim: At the poles each solar year has one day and one night, each about half a year; at the equator day and night are roughly equal, while other regions vary with latitude.

TABATABAI:2:164#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r4.claim: Changing day length alters light and heat and thus the conditions that produce varied terrestrial forms and transformations useful to humans.

TABATABAI:2:164#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#2/r5.claim: Falak means a ship and can denote one or several; its benefit is carrying goods and provisions between shores and regions.

TABATABAI:2:164#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r1.claim: Human crafts depend on God as do natural things. An idol’s material existence is God-created, while its status as an object worshipped besides God belongs to human or satanic action.

TABATABAI:2:164#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r2.claim: Manufactured things are attributable to creation just like natural things, in proportion to their existence.

TABATABAI:2:164#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r3.claim: Rain develops through evaporation, condensation and precipitation as rain, snow, or hail; it nourishes Earth and sustains plants and animals, and, as part of the connected world, points to one creator who is also humanity’s God.

TABATABAI:2:164#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:164#3/r4.claim: Wind is air displaced by unequal solar heating: warmed, lighter air rises as cooler, heavier air moves in and pushes it along; wind pollinates plants, disperses vapor and decay, and carries rain clouds.

TABATABAI:2:164-165/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:164-165/r1.speaker: author
